What does BACA do? Part III
Proposed CEQA ballot initiative would prevent changing environmental standards very early in the development process.
This is the third in a series of blog posts on the California Chamber of Commerce’s proposed ballot initiative (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0023A1%20%28%26quot%3BEssential%20Projects%26quot%3B%29.pdf) amending the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). The first blog post is here (https://legal-planet.org/2026/02/25/what-does-the-building-an-affordable-california-act-do/). The second blog post is here (https://legal-planet.org/2026/02/26/what-does-baca-do-part-ii/).
The most sweeping change in the initiative is buried in the lead-in to an innocuously titled section, proposed new Section 21023 “Other Public Agency Actions for Essential Projects.”
Here is the key text, in the beginning of 21023(a)
“If an essential project requires any other public agency action that is not expressly addressed by other provisions of this chapter, the public agency shall make a final written decision thereon based on compliance with existing laws.”
What this means is that any approval – even if it has nothing to do with CEQA – must be made pursuant to “compliance with existing laws.” What does “existing laws” mean? That term is defined in proposed new Section 21028(r)(1):
“Formally adopted legal requirements contained in statutes, regulations, rules, standards, or ordinances that existed and were in effect on the date an application for an essential project was submitted to a public agency.”
Thus, only the law in place at the time an application is submitted to an agency can be applied to review of a project. This is what lawyers call “vested rights” – a constraint on the ability of the government to change the rules for a project after a certain point in time. California recognizes vested rights, but in general the trigger for vested rights in California is substantially later in time than the submission of an application. And for good reason.
Early vested rights provide certainty and predictability for project proponents. Those are good things. But they come with costs.
First, it prevents the government from responding to changed circumstances. For instance, if the environmental review of a project identifies a new harm not currently covered in existing written standards, there is nothing the government can do to prevent that harm. This may be particularly an issue when a proponent proposes a dramatically new type of project, or is proposing a project in a location without preexisting environmental data.
The initiative does provide a very limited exception to address this issue, but only “to mitigate or avoid a specific, adverse life-safety impact, meaning a significant, quantifiable, direct, and unavoidable life-safety impact, including life-safety impacts associated with new or emerging technologies, materials, or grid-integration systems, and that is based on objective, identified and written public safety standards, policies, or conditions.” (Proposed new Section 21028(r)(2)). If you’re a newly discovered endangered species population, for instance, you may well be out of luck. Or if there is uncertainty about the potential impacts, perhaps because there is not clear information about the risks of the new technology involved, the government may well be unable to act as well.
Second, it may facilitate strategic behavior by project proponents. 21028(r)(1) does not define “submitted” – but it seems to mean when an applicant has submitted an application, any kind of application, to the public agency. (Such a broad interpretation would, of course, be based on Section 21029, which calls for the initiative to be broadly interpreted to allow for approval of covered projects.) So what is to stop an applicant from submitting a proposal with minimal information to a public agency to freeze the relevant law? Sure, the public agency can say the application is incomplete – the initiative has a limited timeframe for the agency to provide such a response, where CEQA is involved – but there is nothing to stop the applicant from dawdling in their response, or providing only a partial response (requiring another reply by the agency), and so freezing the relevant law for an extended period of time. We might even see properties with submitted applications get increased value because of their vested rights.
The vested rights here do not appear to depend on whether CEQA applies to a project. And indeed the scope section for the proposed initiative, proposed new Section 21013, says it applies to all “essential” projects, period, not just to the “essential” projects going through a CEQA process. Thus, these are vested rights for all state and local approval of all covered projects in the state. That breadth belies the claims of the initiative text that it does not “diminish the authority of any public agency to approve or disapprove an essential project.” (Section 21014(a)).
And note that because the initiative states that it overrides any conflicting law, it necessarily overrides any contrary vested rights doctrine in state law for any other statute.
Finally, it is possible the vested rights in the initiative extend beyond the initial approval of the project, and prohibit increasing regulatory standards for any covered project after it is constructed, during its operation. The vested rights provision in 21023(a) covers “any other public agency action that is not expressly addressed by other provisions of this chapter.” Action is not defined in the initiative. But it might include any public agency action that applies at any time to the essential project – proposed new Section 21023(a) on its own terms provides no time limit to its coverage. If that is the case (and again, remember we are to broadly apply the initiative under Section 21029(a) “to afford the fullest possible weight to the interest of . . . essential projects”), then any subsequent regulatory decision for a covered project is bound by vested rights. In other words, the agency and state legislature could never update or make more stringent the regulatory standards that apply to a covered project, in perpetuity . It is a permanent lock-in of all regulatory standards. That would be a drastic – and probably untenable – change in law. Cutting against this interpretation is that overall Section 21023 sets decision timeframes for the “other public agency action” based on the timeframe for the original decision about CEQA applicability or review for the project. Section 21023(a)(1). However, one could also read this provision as implicitly prohibiting any adverse subsequent public agency action with respect to the project, if that action would occur after the deadlines set in Section 21023(a)(1). That would mean that public agencies could not (except at the request of the applicant) make additional regulatory decisions with respect to a covered project after its initial approval – basically achieving the same result of freezing in relevant law.
Of course, this broad vested rights provision is not flagged at all in the preamble to the initiative (which asserts it does not affect existing state environmental laws).

Biber's analysis is substantive but one-sided (he's a pro-CEQA scholar who supports reform but thinks BACA goes too far). Importantly he notes BACA does address real concerns and he proposed alternative reforms.

Now let me consider the counterpoints from the pro side with legal expertise. Let me look at:
- Daily Journal "The devil in the details of Prop 45" (opponents' view?) and "Prop 45 will speed data center construction" (McKerley & Frank).
- Pro-side legal analysis: Sean Marciniak (Hanson Bridgett, helped draft), and maybe an op-ed by Jason Elliott in CalMatters (July 2026) — "Californians have a rare chance to rein in CEQA and support housing" (LA Times contributor).

Also worth checking: what happened to the outcome? Today appears to be around Nov 3, 2026 (election day). Some sources are dated Nov 2-3, 2026. The question is what to vote. I should make a judgment based on the merits.

Key considerations for decision:

Arguments for YES:
1. CEQA is genuinely abused for delay and NIMBY purposes; litigation adds costs, delays housing, hospitals, clean energy, wildfire mitigation, water projects.
2. California has a severe housing affordability crisis; construction cost/time premiums are large ($75k/home claimed).
3. Deadlines with enforcement create accountability; the optional nature means applicants choose.
4. Broad coalition support: hospitals, water association, affordable housing council, LULAC, Hispanic chambers, building industry, clean energy groups, Farm Bureau.
5. Many newspaper endorsements (26 papers + WSJ).

Arguments for NO:
1. The measure is far broader than deadlines: it freezes regulatory standards at application date (vested rights) across ALL state and local approvals, potentially in perpetuity; limits alternatives analysis to a single applicant-proposed alternative; caps public comment at 45 days; excludes late comments from judicial record; narrows judicial review (court can only invalidate part of project); limits tribal consultation to federally recognized tribes; includes an interpretation clause giving "fullest possible weight" to approving essential projects; overrides conflicting laws.
2. Housing is already largely exempt via AB 130/SB 131 (2025), which is producing results (17,913 units in 15 months). So the marginal housing benefit is smaller, while covering greenfield sprawl housing, freeways, logging, dams, possibly data centers (via "ancillary" infrastructure and broadband definitions).
3. It's a 41-page initiative statute that can't be amended except by 2/3 vote and only to further its purposes — a one-way ratchet that locks in drafting errors and unforeseen consequences.
4. Legal experts (Biber at Berkeley, Sivas at Stanford, Stein at UCLA, Frank) warn of unintended, sweeping effects, including possibly eliminating CEQA protections for endangered species habitat and cumulative air pollution in EJ communities — at a time when the federal government is rolling back the ESA/NEPA.
5. The Legislature was actively working on CEQA reform (Newsom vetoed a bill; the Senate passed BAAJA-type reform?) — better to do targeted reform through legislation that can be adjusted.
6. Fiscal cost: up to $100M+/yr initially for state/local governments and courts.
7. Key pro-housing/YIMBY groups (California YIMBY, SPUR, Abundant Housing LA, YIMBY Action) refused to endorse — neutral; Greenbelt Alliance and Eastbay for Everyone oppose. Scott Wiener neutral. Tom Steyer opposes. Even Rural County Representatives (historically pro-CEQA reform) stayed neutral, with policy advocate saying it goes too far.
8. The "affordability" claim is not guaranteed — no affordability requirement; savings estimates come from a Chamber-commissioned study; the $75k/home figure comes from the Building Industry Association.
9. The measure shifts power from communities/agencies to applicants; the "fullest possible weight" clause tilts ambiguity toward approval.
10. Polling: support fell from 73% to 46% once voters learned details; now trailing 46-50.

Consider also: Is there a "less bad" path? A no vote doesn't stop CEQA reform — the Legislature has repeatedly passed streamlining and could continue; there's also a federal permitting reform bill (BAAJA). Yes campaign is heavily funded by utilities (PG&E), oil company (California Resources Corp), tech companies, data center builders, developers.

Given the significant drafting risk, the lock-in provision, the breadth beyond housing (freeways, logging, dams, sprawl), the erosion of tribal consultation, the vested rights freeze, and the fact that the targeted housing fix (AB 130) is already working, a "no" seems the better-supported choice on the merits. Notably, most independent legal scholars who studied the text (Biber, Sivas, Stein, Frank, and some land-use attorneys) found it goes well beyond streamlining; the LAO flags substantive changes beyond timelines; the nonpartisan rural-county group declined to support it.

But let me weigh the yes side more fairly. Let me check a couple more sources: (a) Daily Journal articles (both pro and con legal analyses), (b) the LA Times contributor op-ed by a pro-side author, (c) maybe an op-ed from Jason Elliott, (d) whether any prominent progressives/YIMBYs support it (e.g., Ezra Klein? Derek Thompson? "Abundance" crowd). Ezra Klein wrote about permitting reform. Let me search whether prominent abundance advocates endorsed Prop 45 — e.g., Ezra Klein, Matt Yglesias, Keith Whitaker, Marc Dunkelman. Arguments for YES:
1. CEQA is genuinely abused for delay and NIMBY purposes; litigation adds costs, delays housing, hospitals, clean energy, wildfire mitigation, water projects.
2. California has a severe housing affordability crisis; construction cost/time premiums are large ($75k/home claimed).
3. Deadlines with enforcement create accountability; the optional nature means applicants choose.
4. Broad coalition support: hospitals, water association, affordable housing council, LULAC, Hispanic chambers, building industry, clean energy groups, Farm Bureau.
5. Many newspaper endorsements (26 papers + WSJ).

Arguments for NO:
1. The measure is far broader than deadlines: it freezes regulatory standards at application date (vested rights) across ALL state and local approvals, potentially in perpetuity; limits alternatives analysis to a single applicant-proposed alternative; caps public comment at 45 days; excludes late comments from judicial record; narrows judicial review (court can only invalidate part of project); limits tribal consultation to federally recognized tribes; includes an interpretation clause giving "fullest possible weight" to approving essential projects; overrides conflicting laws.
2. Housing is already largely exempt via AB 130/SB 131 (2025), which is producing results (17,913 units in 15 months). So the marginal housing benefit is smaller, while covering greenfield sprawl housing, freeways, logging, dams, possibly data centers (via "ancillary" infrastructure and broadband definitions).
3. It's a 41-page initiative statute that can't be amended except by 2/3 vote and only to further its purposes — a one-way ratchet that locks in drafting errors and unforeseen consequences.
4. Legal experts (Biber at Berkeley, Sivas at Stanford, Stein at UCLA, Frank) warn of unintended, sweeping effects, including possibly eliminating CEQA protections for endangered species habitat and cumulative air pollution in EJ communities — at a time when the federal government is rolling back the ESA/NEPA.
5. The Legislature was actively working on CEQA reform (Newsom vetoed a bill; the Senate passed BAAJA-type reform?) — better to do targeted reform through legislation that can be adjusted.
6. Fiscal cost: up to $100M+/yr initially for state/local governments and courts.
7. Key pro-housing/YIMBY groups (California YIMBY, SPUR, Abundant Housing LA, YIMBY Action) refused to endorse — neutral; Greenbelt Alliance and Eastbay for Everyone oppose. Scott Wiener neutral. Tom Steyer opposes. Even Rural County Representatives (historically pro-CEQA reform) stayed neutral, with policy advocate saying it goes too far.
8. The "affordability" claim is not guaranteed — no affordability requirement; savings estimates come from a Chamber-commissioned study; the $75k/home figure comes from the Building Industry Association.
9. The measure shifts power from communities/agencies to applicants; the "fullest possible weight" clause tilts ambiguity toward approval.
10. Polling: support fell from 73% to 46% once voters learned details; now trailing 46-50.

Consider also: Is there a "less bad" path? A no vote doesn't stop CEQA reform — the Legislature has repeatedly passed streamlining and could continue; there's also a federal permitting reform bill (BAAJA). Yes campaign is heavily funded by utilities (PG&E), oil company (California Resources Corp), tech companies, data center builders, developers.

Notably, most independent legal scholars who studied the text (Biber, Sivas, Stein, Frank, and some land-use attorneys) found it goes well beyond streamlining; the LAO flags substantive changes beyond timelines; the nonpartisan rural-county group declined to support it.

Biber's analysis is substantive but one-sided (he's a pro-CEQA scholar who supports reform but thinks BACA goes too far). Importantly he notes BACA does address real concerns and he proposed alternative reforms.

Now let me consider the counterpoints from the pro side with legal expertise. Let me look at:
- Daily Journal "The devil in the details of Prop 45" (opponents' view?) and "Prop 45 will speed data center construction" (McKerley & Frank).
- Pro-side legal analysis: Sean Marciniak (Hanson Bridgett, helped draft), and maybe an op-ed by Jason Elliott in CalMatters (July 2026) — "Californians have a rare chance to rein in CEQA and support housing" (LA Times contributor).

Also worth checking: what happened to the outcome? Today appears to be around Nov 3, 2026 (election day). Some sources are dated Nov 2-3, 2026. The question is what to vote. I should make a judgment based on the merits.

Key considerations for decision:

Arguments for YES:
1. CEQA is genuinely abused for delay and NIMBY purposes; litigation adds costs, delays housing, hospitals, clean energy, wildfire mitigation, water projects.
2. California has a severe housing affordability crisis; construction cost/time premiums are large ($75k/home claimed).
3. Deadlines with enforcement create accountability; the optional nature means applicants choose.
4. Broad coalition support: hospitals, water association, affordable housing council, LULAC, Hispanic chambers, building industry, clean energy groups, Farm Bureau.
5. Many newspaper endorsements (26 papers + WSJ).

Arguments for NO:
1. The measure is far broader than deadlines: it freezes regulatory standards at application date (vested rights) across ALL state and local approvals, potentially in perpetuity; limits alternatives analysis to a single applicant-proposed alternative; caps public comment at 45 days; excludes late comments from judicial record; narrows judicial review (court can only invalidate part of project); limits tribal consultation to federally recognized tribes; includes an interpretation clause giving "fullest possible weight" to approving essential projects; overrides conflicting laws.
2. Housing is already largely exempt via AB 130/SB 131 (2025), which is producing results (17,913 units in 15 months). So the marginal housing benefit is smaller, while covering greenfield sprawl housing, freeways, logging, dams, possibly data centers (via "ancillary" infrastructure and broadband definitions).
3. It's a 41-page initiative statute that can't be amended except by 2/3 vote and only to further its purposes — a one-way ratchet that locks in drafting errors and unforeseen consequences.
4. Legal experts (Biber at Berkeley, Sivas at Stanford, Stein at UCLA, Frank) warn of unintended, sweeping effects, including possibly eliminating CEQA protections for endangered species habitat and cumulative air pollution in EJ communities — at a time when the federal government is rolling back the ESA/NEPA.
5. The Legislature was actively working on CEQA reform (Newsom vetoed a bill; the Senate passed BAAJA-type reform?) — better to do targeted reform through legislation that can be adjusted.
6. Fiscal cost: up to $100M+/yr initially for state/local governments and courts.
7. Key pro-housing/YIMBY groups (California YIMBY, SPUR, Abundant Housing LA, YIMBY Action) refused to endorse — neutral; Greenbelt Alliance and Eastbay for Everyone oppose. Scott Wiener neutral. Tom Steyer opposes. Even Rural County Representatives (historically pro-CEQA reform) stayed neutral, with policy advocate saying it goes too far.
8. The "affordability" claim is not guaranteed — no affordability requirement; savings estimates come from a Chamber-commissioned study; the $75k/home figure comes from the Building Industry Association.
9. The measure shifts power from communities/agencies to applicants; the "fullest possible weight" clause tilts ambiguity toward approval.
10. Polling: support fell from 73% to 46% once voters learned details; now trailing 46-50.

Consider also: Is there a "less bad" path? A no vote doesn't stop CEQA reform — the Legislature has repeatedly passed streamlining and could continue; there's also a federal permitting reform bill (BAAJA). Yes campaign is heavily funded by utilities (PG&E), oil company (California Resources Corp), tech companies, data center builders, developers.

Given the significant drafting risk, the lock-in provision, the breadth beyond housing (freeways, logging, dams, sprawl), the erosion of tribal consultation, the vested rights freeze, and the fact that the targeted housing fix (AB 130) is already working, a "no" seems the better-supported choice on the merits. Notably, most independent legal scholars who studied the text (Biber, Sivas, Stein, Frank, and some land-use attorneys) found it goes well beyond streamlining; the LAO flags substantive changes beyond timelines; the nonpartisan rural-county group declined to support it.

But let me weigh the yes side more fairly. Let me check a couple more sources: (a) Daily Journal articles (both pro and con legal analyses), (b) the LA Times contributor op-ed by a pro-side author, (c) maybe an op-ed from Jason Elliott, (d) whether any prominent progressives/YIMBYs support it (e.g., Ezra Klein? Derek Thompson? "Abundance" crowd). Ezra Klein wrote about permitting reform. Let me search whether prominent abundance advocates endorsed Prop 45 — e.g., Ezra Klein, Matt Yglesias, Keith Whitaker, Marc Dunkelman. Their view matters because the "yes" case is the abundance case.

The debate is highly contested, even among legal experts. The WSJ piece frames it as an abundance test. Let me read the WSJ opinion piece "Do Liberals Really Want 'Abundance'?" and Julia Stein's Daily Journal piece on "the true scope of Prop 45's changes to environmental protection" for the counterweight. Also Sean Marciniak's pro piece.

Also let me check the KQED voter guide and the "Lookout" op-ed from environmental leaders.

Most important for my decision: what is the net expected effect? Let me think about a few key empirical/policy questions:

1. Does CEQA delay meaningfully raise housing costs? Evidence: CEQA litigation targets a small share of projects (~200 lawsuits/year out of thousands of projects); most housing is exempt now (AB 130). The Holland & Knight study says 87% of CEQA lawsuits target infill housing, and 64% of appellate-challenged projects were infill. But CEQA review costs affect a small subset of projects. However, the "shadow" of CEQA influences process design and timelines broadly.

2. Does Prop 45's coverage go beyond what's needed? Yes — it covers essentially all housing (including greenfield), all transportation (except HSR), water, logging/forest management, broadband, etc., with "related and ancillary infrastructure."

3. Risk analysis: The initiative is 41 pages, drafted by interested parties, can only be amended by 2/3 vote, and contains provisions that legal scholars across the spectrum say create major uncertainty and potentially lock in regulatory standards permanently (vested rights). It also weakens judicial review and public comment. Meanwhile the specific problem it claims to solve (housing delay) has already been addressed by AB 130/SB 131 in 2025 with strong early results, and the Legislature is actively engaged in CEQA reform and could pass more targeted reform with a simple majority.

4. Distributional concerns: The measure would remove communities' main tool for challenging polluting projects (freeways, warehouses via ancillary infrastructure, data centers possibly), which disproportionately burden EJ communities. The narrowing of tribal consultation excludes non-federally recognized tribes (a significant share of California tribes) — a serious equity/sovereignty issue flagged by the LA Times.

5. Fiscal: LAO says up-front costs possibly >$100M/yr; long-term uncertain.

6. Political economy: Yes side funded by utilities (PG&E), oil & gas producer (California Resources Corp), data center builders, developers, tech billionaires — interests with a direct stake. No side funded by labor, environmental groups, Wendy Schmidt. Both sides have self-interest; but the Yes side's funding pattern (oil company + data centers) is at least consistent with the concern that the measure's breadth favors polluting projects. Also note that Eric Schmidt (former Google CEO) donated to the Yes committee while data centers are a flashpoint.

Now, on the other hand, the strongest yes case: California's cost of living crisis is severe; delays cost money; CEQA abuse is documented; deadlines are common-sense; and the option to opt in means applicants who want speed accept tradeoffs. Also the argument that the Legislature has failed for decades to do comprehensive reform; Newsom vetoed SB 607? (There was a "CEQA poison pill in SB 607" article by Elkind — SB 607 may have been a reform bill vetoed by Newsom.) If Newsom vetoed a legislative reform, that weakens the "just let the Legislature do it" argument. Let me check what SB 607 was and what Newsom vetoed.

Let me also check whether prominent "abundance" advocates endorsed Prop 45 — e.g., did Ezra Klein write about it? The WSJ article suggests the abundance movement is being tested. Let me search for Klein's take and for a pro-45 op-ed by a liberal/progressive (e.g., Matthew Lewis, Brian Hanlon?).

Let me batch: WSJ article + search for Newsom veto SB 607 CEQA reform 2026.

Distributional concerns: The measure would remove communities' main tool for challenging polluting projects (freeways, warehouses via ancillary infrastructure, data centers possibly), which disproportionately burden EJ communities. The narrowing of tribal consultation excludes non-federally recognized tribes (a significant share of California tribes) — a serious equity/sovereignty issue flagged by the LA Times.

5. Fiscal: LAO says up-front costs possibly >$100M/yr; long-term uncertain.

6. Political economy: Yes side funded by utilities (PG&E), oil & gas producer (California Resources Corp), data center builders, developers, tech billionaires — interests with a direct stake. Also note that Eric Schmidt (former Google CEO) donated to the Yes committee while data centers are a flashpoint.

The debate is highly contested, even among legal experts. The WSJ piece frames it as an abundance test. Let me read the WSJ opinion piece "Do Liberals Really Want 'Abundance'?" and Julia Stein's Daily Journal piece on "the true scope of Prop 45's changes to environmental protection" for the counterweight. Also Sean Marciniak's pro piece.

Also let me check the KQED voter guide and the "Lookout" op-ed from environmental leaders.

Most important for my decision: what is the net expected effect? Let me think about a few key empirical/policy questions:

1. Does CEQA delay meaningfully raise housing costs? Evidence: CEQA litigation targets a small share of projects (~200 lawsuits/year out of thousands of projects); most housing is exempt now (AB 130). The Holland & Knight study says 87% of CEQA lawsuits target infill housing, and 64% of appellate-challenged projects were infill. But CEQA review costs affect a small subset of projects. However, the "shadow" of CEQA influences process design and timelines broadly.

2. Does Prop 45's coverage go beyond what's needed? Yes — it covers essentially all housing (including greenfield), all transportation (except HSR), water, logging/forest management, broadband, etc., with "related and ancillary infrastructure."

3. Risk analysis: The initiative is 41 pages, drafted by interested parties, can only be amended by 2/3 vote, and contains provisions that legal scholars across the spectrum say create major uncertainty and potentially lock in regulatory standards permanently (vested rights). It also weakens judicial review and public comment. Meanwhile the specific problem it claims to solve (housing delay) has already been addressed by AB 130/SB 131 in 2025 with strong early results, and the Legislature is actively engaged in CEQA reform and could pass more targeted reform with a simple majority.

4. Distributional concerns: The measure would remove communities' main tool for challenging polluting projects (freeways, warehouses via ancillary infrastructure, data centers possibly), which disproportionately burden EJ communities. The narrowing of tribal consultation excludes non-federally recognized tribes (a significant share of California tribes) — a serious equity/sovereignty issue flagged by the LA Times.

5. Fiscal: LAO says up-front costs possibly >$100M/yr; long-term uncertain.

6. Political economy: Yes side funded by utilities (PG&E), oil & gas producer (California Resources Corp), data center builders, developers, tech billionaires — interests with a direct stake. No side funded by labor, environmental groups, Wendy Schmidt. Both sides have self-interest; but the Yes side's funding pattern (oil company + data centers) is at least consistent with the concern that the measure's breadth favors polluting projects. Also note that Eric Schmidt (former Google CEO) donated to the Yes committee while data centers are a flashpoint.

Now, on the other hand, the strongest yes case: California's cost of living crisis is severe; delays cost money; CEQA abuse is documented; deadlines are common-sense; and the option to opt in means applicants who want speed accept tradeoffs. Also the argument that the Legislature has failed for decades to do comprehensive reform; Newsom vetoed SB 607? (There was a "CEQA poison pill in SB 607" article by Elkind — SB 607 may have been a reform bill vetoed by Newsom.) If Newsom vetoed a legislative reform, that weakens the "just let the Legislature do it" argument. Let me check what SB 607 was and what Newsom vetoed.

Let me also check whether prominent "abundance" advocates endorsed Prop 45 — e.g., did Ezra Klein write about it? The WSJ article suggests the abundance movement is being tested. Let me search for Klein's take and for a pro-45 op-ed by a liberal/progressive (e.g., Matthew Lewis, Brian Hanlon?).

Notable: Newsom vetoed SB 954 (which would have narrowed the manufacturing exemption) — showing the political environment favors streamlining. Also Newsom stayed silent on Prop 45.

Key fact: The Legislature is demonstrably active on CEQA reform (AB 130, SB 131 in 2025; ongoing work; a Senate permitting reform bill at the federal level). And notably, the California Legislature could respond to a "no" vote with more targeted reform; whereas a "yes" vote locks in a 41-page statute amendable only by 2/3.

Let me also examine the "yes" case at its strongest from an expert: Sean Marciniak's Daily Journal piece and the "lookout" op-eds. And I want to check whether the measure contains provisions that could be considered beneficial: e.g., prevailing wage requirements for non-housing essential projects (Section 21028 labor requirements — applying 21183.5 prevailing wage). That's a labor protection; but housing projects only need prevailing wage for buildings over 85 feet — which is a weakening relative to... hmm, actually under AB 130's streamlining, prevailing wage applies. So Prop 45 keeps some labor standards. The California Labor Federation opposes anyway.

Another consideration: the measure gives applicants the option to use it. If it's bad, applicants wouldn't use it? But applicants will use it whenever beneficial, so the selection effect means it will be used where it most tilts the balance.

Let me read the LA Times "last-minute guide" and the Lookout op-ed from environmental leaders ("California has already streamlined CEQA. Proposition 45 goes too far") — which may be signed by mainstream environmentalists (e.g., Save the Redwoods, etc.), plus Julia Stein's Daily Journal piece for the legal scope of environmental protection changes.

Also, let me check the KQED voter guide for a balanced summary, and possibly a pro-45 expert analysis (e.g., from the Pacific Legal Foundation or Reason).

Proposition 45
Should California speed up its environmental review process for certain projects?
The proposition would amend the state’s landmark environmental review law, the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA), to expedite specific “essential” projects, including housing, transportation, water, health, wildfire mitigation, educational buildings, internet access and clean energy projects. It would set a 365-day time limit on these environmental reviews and require courts to rule on CEQA-related lawsuits within 270 days. There is debate as to whether its language could be construed to include data centers.
Yes Argument
California’s system for approving housing, water, clean energy, roads, schools, hospitals and wildfire prevention is too slow, bureaucratic and costly. Proposition 45 would set enforceable timelines for project approvals, streamline legal challenges and reduce frivolous lawsuits. Projects would still undergo environmental review and cities and counties could still approve or deny them. The proposition excludes Delta conveyance, nuclear power and high-speed rail projects.
No Argument
Proposition 45 limits the environmental review of major development projects and the public’s right to be heard. It reduces public agency requirements to consider public comments on proposed projects — comments that often expose potential contamination of air and water or damage to our coast, rivers and wildlife. It was written by a business group and financed by gas and electric utilities and corporate PACs.

Proposition 45
Should California speed up its environmental review process for certain projects?
The proposition would amend the state’s landmark environmental review law, the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA), to expedite specific “essential” projects, including housing, transportation, water, health, wildfire mitigation, educational buildings, internet access and clean energy projects. It would set a 365-day time limit on these environmental reviews and require courts to rule on CEQA-related lawsuits within 270 days. There is debate as to whether its language could be construed to include data centers.
Yes Argument
California’s system for approving housing, water, clean energy, roads, schools, hospitals and wildfire prevention is too slow, bureaucratic and costly. Proposition 45 would set enforceable timelines for project approvals, streamline legal challenges and reduce frivolous lawsuits. Projects would still undergo environmental review and cities and counties could still approve or deny them. The proposition excludes Delta conveyance, nuclear power and high-speed rail projects.
No Argument
Proposition 45 limits the environmental review of major development projects and the public’s right to be heard. It reduces public agency requirements to consider public comments on proposed projects — comments that often expose potential contamination of air and water or damage to our coast, rivers and wildlife. It was written by a business group and financed by gas and electric utilities and corporate PACs.

Notable: Newsom vetoed SB 954 (which would have narrowed the manufacturing exemption) — showing the political environment favors streamlining. Also Newsom stayed silent on Prop 45.

Key fact: The Legislature is demonstrably active on CEQA reform (AB 130, SB 131 in 2025; ongoing work; a Senate permitting reform bill at the federal level). And notably, the California Legislature could respond to a "no" vote with more targeted reform; whereas a "yes" vote locks in a 41-page statute amendable only by 2/3.

Let me also examine the "yes" case at its strongest from an expert: Sean Marciniak's Daily Journal piece and the "lookout" op-eds. And I want to check whether the measure contains provisions that could be considered beneficial: e.g., prevailing wage requirements for non-housing essential projects (Section 21028 labor requirements — applying 21183.5 prevailing wage). That's a labor protection; but housing projects only need prevailing wage for buildings over 85 feet — which is a weakening relative to... hmm, actually under AB 130's streamlining, prevailing wage applies. So Prop 45 keeps some labor standards. The California Labor Federation opposes anyway.

Another consideration: the measure gives applicants the option to use it. If it's bad, applicants wouldn't use it? But applicants will use it whenever beneficial, so the selection effect means it will be used where it most tilts the balance.

Let me read the LA Times "last-minute guide" and the Lookout op-ed from environmental leaders ("California has already streamlined CEQA. Proposition 45 goes too far") — which may be signed by mainstream environmentalists (e.g., Save the Redwoods, etc.), plus Julia Stein's Daily Journal piece for the legal scope of environmental protection changes.

Also, let me check the KQED voter guide for a balanced summary, and possibly a pro-45 expert analysis (e.g., from the Pacific Legal Foundation or Reason).

Proposition 45
Should California speed up its environmental review process for certain projects?
The proposition would amend the state’s landmark environmental review law, the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA), to expedite specific “essential” projects, including housing, transportation, water, health, wildfire mitigation, educational buildings, internet access and clean energy projects. It would set a 365-day time limit on these environmental reviews and require courts to rule on CEQA-related lawsuits within 270 days. There is debate as to whether its language could be construed to include data centers.
Yes Argument
California’s system for approving housing, water, clean energy, roads, schools, hospitals and wildfire prevention is too slow, bureaucratic and costly. Proposition 45 would set enforceable timelines for project approvals, streamline legal challenges and reduce frivolous lawsuits. Projects would still undergo environmental review and cities and counties could still approve or deny them. The proposition excludes Delta conveyance, nuclear power and high-speed rail projects.
No Argument
Proposition 45 limits the environmental review of major development projects and the public’s right to be heard. It reduces public agency requirements to consider public comments on proposed projects — comments that often expose potential contamination of air and water or damage to our coast, rivers and wildlife. It was written by a business group and financed by gas and electric utilities and corporate PACs.

21027. Timelines and Processes Applicable to
Judicial Review of Essential Project Approvals or
Authorizations
(a) Timelines.
(1) (A) An action or proceeding, to attack, review, set
aside, void, or annul a public agency’s approval or
authorization of an essential project shall be
commenced within 30 days from the date the public
agency files a notice of determination or notice of
exemption pursuant to Section 21108 or 21152. The
action or proceeding shall be completed within 270
days, inclusive of original and appellate court
proceedings, pursuant to the judicial streamlining
procedures applicable to environmental leadership
development projects pursuant to Section 21185.
(B) The court may, in its own discretion, extend the
270-day deadline contained in subparagraph (A) by up
to an additional 90 days.
(2) Notwithstanding any contrary provision in Section
21185 or any rule adopted by the Judicial Council, and
except as provided in subparagraph (B) of paragraph
(1), the 270-day deadline in paragraph (1) shall only be
extended upon mutual written consent of the plaintiff or
petitioner, the public agency, and the applicant.
(b) Administrative Record.
The whole administrative record consists only of
notices, studies, and other documents consistent with
both of the following:
(1) Documents required under this division to be sent
or distributed to members of the public by the lead

agency, made available to the public at a public

(2) With respect to public comments, comments
described in subdivision (d) of Section 21021, and
responses and comments described in subdivision (e)
of Section 21021.
(c) Remedies.
(1) If the court finds, as a result of a trial, hearing, or
remand from an appellate court, that a public agency’s
approval or authorization of an essential project is not
supported by substantial evidence in the record, the
court shall issue an order and peremptory writ of
mandate explaining the deficiency with specificity as to
which requirement of this division or the state CEQA
Guidelines with which the approval or authorization
does not comply, and identify what part, phase, or
activity of an essential project was affected by the
noncompliance.
(2) The remedy shall be limited only to prohibiting
commencement of the noncomplying part, phase, or
activity until the noncompliance is corrected.
(3) When those required corrective actions have been
completed, the public agency shall file a return to the
writ affirming compliance, and the court shall thereafter
dismiss the action or proceeding. A court may not order
or direct via writ or any other form of order, injunction,
or decision that a public agency rescind its approval or
authorization of the essential project.
(4) Any essential project part, phase, or activity not
within the scope of the deficiency identified in the writ
shall not be subject to the writ, and is not subject to
further challenge in an action or proceeding under this
division.
(d) Subsequent Approvals or Authorizations.
(1) No further action or proceeding to challenge the
implementation through completion of construction or
subsequent approval or authorization of an essential
project, or portion of an essential project, may be filed if
the public agency’s approval or authorization was not
subject to a judicial challenge, the public agency
approval or authorization was challenged and upheld,
or the public agency has filed a return to the writ that
has been accepted as satisfactory by the court pursuant
to subdivision (c).
(2) Minor modifications to an essential project that do
not result in any new significant impacts, or that do not
substantially worsen any previously identified
significant impacts, of the initially approved essential
project, may not be challenged in an action or
proceeding under this division.
45 (e) Injunctive Relief.
(1) Upon a showing by clear and convincing evidence
that an essential project would have a specific, adverse
impact upon public safety, and there is no feasible
method to satisfactorily mitigate or avoid the specific,
adverse impact upon public safety, a court may order
that construction or completion of the particular

specific, adverse impact upon public safety be halted or
prohibited solely by issuing a temporary injunction.
(2) For purposes of paragraph (1), satisfactory
mitigation to avoid the specific, adverse impact upon
public safety shall be deemed to exist upon either of the
following:
(A) A public agency’s subsequent decision to modify
the essential project to avoid or mitigate to a less than
significant level that specific, adverse public safety
impact and that decision shall not require the agency to
take any further action under this division.
(B) A public agency’s determination that the specific,

mitigated to a less than significant level following
preparation of an environmental impact report or
supplemental environmental impact report addressing
only that specific, adverse public safety impact
pursuant to the timelines and procedures set forth in

Article 7. Definitions
21028. Definitions
For purposes of this chapter, the following definitions
apply:
(a) “Applicant” means a person, legal entity, public
agency, or public utility that proposes an essential
project.
(b) “Approval or authorization” means any approval,
authorization, determination, finding, financing, real
property transaction or contract, or other public agency
actions that further the advancement, construction,
completion, or realization of an essential project.
(c) “California educational institution” means all of the
following: a school district; a county superintendent of
schools; a county board of education; a community
college district; a state special school; the Board of
Governors of the California Community Colleges or the
Chancellor of the California Community Colleges; the
California State University or the Board of Trustees of
the California State University; the University of
California or the Regents of the University of California;
the University of California Law San Francisco, formerly
Hastings College of the Law; a charter school
established pursuant to the Charter Schools Act of
1992 (Part 26.8 (commencing with Section 47600) of
Division 4 of Title 2 of the Education Code); and a
nonprofit college or university with membership in the
Association of Independent California Colleges and
Universities.
(d) “CEQA” means the California Environmental Quality
Act (Division 13 (commencing with Section 21000)).
(e) (1) “Consulting tribe” means a tribe that appears
on the most recent list published by the United States
pursuant to the Federally Recognized Indian Tribe List
Act of 1994 (25 U.S.C. Sec. 5131), and is traditionally
and culturally affiliated with the geographic area of the
proposed essential project.

(ii) For purposes of this section, “associated

(B) Producing, generating, storing, transmitting, or

(l) “Essential housing project” means all of the

extended upon mutual written consent of the plaintiff or

or direct via writ or any other form of order, injunction,

(4) Any essential project part, phase, or activity not

further challenge in an action or proceeding under this

approval or authorization was challenged and upheld,

(2) In any action or proceeding, to attack, review, set
aside, void, or annul a public agency’s approval or
authorization of an essential project on the grounds that
it has been made without completing the public
participation procedures, the court shall only determine
whether the failure to comply with the public
participation procedures was arbitrary and capricious
and resulted in prejudicial error.
(3) Nothing in this division or the state CEQA Guidelines
shall be applied or construed as imposing procedural or
substantive requirements beyond those explicitly set
forth in this division or the state CEQA Guidelines as
modified or limited by the provisions of this chapter.
(d) Nothing in this article shall be construed to
supersede Sections 1756 and 1759 of the Public
Utilities Code, or any other provision of law governing
judicial review of orders or decisions of the Public
Utilities Commission.
21027. Timelines and Processes Applicable to
Judicial Review of Essential Project Approvals or
Authorizations
(a) Timelines.
(1) (A) An action or proceeding, to attack, review, set
aside, void, or annul a public agency’s approval or
authorization of an essential project shall be
commenced within 30 days from the date the public
agency files a notice of determination or notice of
exemption pursuant to Section 21108 or 21152. The
action or proceeding shall be completed within 270
days, inclusive of original and appellate court
proceedings, pursuant to the judicial streamlining
procedures applicable to environmental leadership
development projects pursuant to Section 21185.
(B) The court may, in its own discretion, extend the
270-day deadline contained in subparagraph (A) by up
to an additional 90 days.
(2) Notwithstanding any contrary provision in Section
21185 or any rule adopted by the Judicial Council, and
except as provided in subparagraph (B) of paragraph
(1), the 270-day deadline in paragraph (1) shall only be
extended upon mutual written consent of the plaintiff or
petitioner, the public agency, and the applicant.
(b) Administrative Record.
The whole administrative record consists only of
notices, studies, and other documents consistent with
both of the following:
(1) Documents required under this division to be sent
or distributed to members of the public by the lead
Text of Proposed Laws | 167
45
TEXT OF PROPOSED LAWS PROPOSITION 45 CONTINUED
agency, made available to the public at a public
repository such as a library, or included on the internet
website of the lead agency.
(2) With respect to public comments, comments
described in subdivision (d) of Section 21021, and
responses and comments described in subdivision (e)
of Section 21021.
(c) Remedies.
(1) If the court finds, as a result of a trial, hearing, or
remand from an appellate court, that a public agency’s
approval or authorization of an essential project is not
supported by substantial evidence in the record, the
court shall issue an order and peremptory writ of
mandate explaining the deficiency with specificity as to
which requirement of this division or the state CEQA
Guidelines with which the approval or authorization
does not comply, and identify what part, phase, or
activity of an essential project was affected by the
noncompliance.
(2) The remedy shall be limited only to prohibiting
commencement of the noncomplying part, phase, or
activity until the noncompliance is corrected.
(3) When those required corrective actions have been
completed, the public agency shall file a return to the
writ affirming compliance, and the court shall thereafter
dismiss the action or proceeding. A court may not order
or direct via writ or any other form of order, injunction,
or decision that a public agency rescind its approval or
authorization of the essential project.
(4) Any essential project part, phase, or activity not
within the scope of the deficiency identified in the writ
shall not be subject to the writ, and is not subject to
further challenge in an action or proceeding under this
division.
(d) Subsequent Approvals or Authorizations.
(1) No further action or proceeding to challenge the
implementation through completion of construction or
subsequent approval or authorization of an essential
project, or portion of an essential project, may be filed if
the public agency’s approval or authorization was not
subject to a judicial challenge, the public agency
approval or authorization was challenged and upheld,
or the public agency has filed a return to the writ that
has been accepted as satisfactory by the court pursuant
to subdivision (c).
(2) Minor modifications to an essential project that do
not result in any new significant impacts, or that do not
substantially worsen any previously identified
significant impacts, of the initially approved essential
project, may not be challenged in an action or
proceeding under this division.
45 (e) Injunctive Relief.
(1) Upon a showing by clear and convincing evidence
that an essential project would have a specific, adverse
impact upon public safety, and there is no feasible
method to satisfactorily mitigate or avoid the specific,
adverse impact upon public safety, a court may order
that construction or completion of the particular
168 | Text of Proposed Laws
essential project component that would result in the
specific, adverse impact upon public safety be halted or
prohibited solely by issuing a temporary injunction.
(2) For purposes of paragraph (1), satisfactory
mitigation to avoid the specific, adverse impact upon
public safety shall be deemed to exist upon either of the
following:
(A) A public agency’s subsequent decision to modify
the essential project to avoid or mitigate to a less than
significant level that specific, adverse public safety
impact and that decision shall not require the agency to
take any further action under this division.
(B) A public agency’s determination that the specific,
adverse impact upon public safety cannot be avoided or
mitigated to a less than significant level following
preparation of an environmental impact report or
supplemental environmental impact report addressing
only that specific, adverse public safety impact
pursuant to the timelines and procedures set forth in
this chapter.
Article 7. Definitions
21028. Definitions
For purposes of this chapter, the following definitions
apply:
(a) “Applicant” means a person, legal entity, public
agency, or public utility that proposes an essential
project.
(b) “Approval or authorization” means any approval,
authorization, determination, finding, financing, real
property transaction or contract, or other public agency
actions that further the advancement, construction,
completion, or realization of an essential project.
(c) “California educational institution” means all of the
following: a school district; a county superintendent of
schools; a county board of education; a community
college district; a state special school; the Board of
Governors of the California Community Colleges or the
Chancellor of the California Community Colleges; the
California State University or the Board of Trustees of
the California State University; the University of
California or the Regents of the University of California;
the University of California Law San Francisco, formerly
Hastings College of the Law; a charter school
established pursuant to the Charter Schools Act of
1992 (Part 26.8 (commencing with Section 47600) of
Division 4 of Title 2 of the Education Code); and a
nonprofit college or university with membership in the
Association of Independent California Colleges and
Universities.
(d) “CEQA” means the California Environmental Quality
Act (Division 13 (commencing with Section 21000)).
(e) (1) “Consulting tribe” means a tribe that appears
on the most recent list published by the United States
pursuant to the Federally Recognized Indian Tribe List
Act of 1994 (25 U.S.C. Sec. 5131), and is traditionally
and culturally affiliated with the geographic area of the
proposed essential project.
TEXT OF PROPOSED LAWS PROPOSITION 45 CONTINUED
(2) Notwithstanding Section 21073 or any other law,
“California Native American tribe” as used in, or with
respect to, Sections 21074, 21080.3.1, 21080.3.2,
21082.3, 21084.2, 21084.3, and this chapter, shall
instead mean, and be read as, “consulting tribe” when
the project is an essential project.
(f) “Day” means both of the following:
(1) As used in Sections 21018 and 21019, “day”
means any day other than a Saturday, Sunday, or any
day designated as a state holiday.
(2) As used in any section of this chapter except for
Sections 21018 and 21019, “day” means a calendar
day.
(g) “Educational facility” means any real property,
facility, structure, building, or fixture that is owned or
operated, or will be owned or operated upon completion,
by one or more California educational institutions for
educational purposes.
(h) “Environmental review document” or
“environmental review documentation” means initial
studies; negative declarations; mitigated negative
declarations; draft and final environmental impact
reports; documents prepared as substitutes for
environmental impact reports; negative declaration and
mitigated negative declarations pursuant to a program
certified pursuant to Section 21080.5; documents or
documentation used to substantiate the applicability of
statutory or categorial exemptions from this division or
streamlining provisions that include, without limitation,
those pursuant to Sections 21083.3 and 21094.5;
addenda and other supplemental or subsequent review
documents; documents prepared under the National
Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (42 U.S.C. Sec. 4321
et seq.) and used by a public agency in the place of any
of the foregoing documents or documentation; and
environmental documents as defined in Section 15361
of Title 14 of the California Code of Regulations.
(i) (1) “Essential broadband internet access project”
means a project to provide massmarket retail service by
wire service, wireless service, or radio to customers in
this state that provides the capability to transmit data
to, and receive data from, all or substantially all internet
endpoints, including, but not limited to, any capabilities
that are incidental to and enable the operation of the
communications service, excluding dial-up internet
access service.
(2) An “essential broadband internet access project”
shall comply with all labor requirements described in
Section 21183.5.
(j) (1) “Essential clean energy project” means a project
that supports California’s climate, energy efficiency,
reliability, electrification, sustainability, or clean energy
objectives through one or more of the following:
(A) (i) Producing, generating, or storing electricity
derived from renewable or sustainable resources,
including, but not limited to, solar, wind, geothermal,
fuel cells that comply with the emissions standards
adopted by the State Air Resources Board pursuant to
the distributed generation certification program
requirements of Section 94203 of Title 17 of the
California Code of Regulations, small hydroelectric
generation of 30 megawatts or less, digester gas,
municipal solid waste conversion, landfill gas, ocean
wave, ocean thermal, or tidal current, and associated
transmission lines.
(ii) For purposes of this section, “associated
transmission lines” means a transmission line that is
required for the interconnection or delivery of electricity
from a facility described in clause (i).
(iii) Notwithstanding clause (i), this subparagraph
excludes producing or generating electricity from
nuclear power.
(B) Producing, generating, storing, transmitting, or
distributing clean hydrogen that is not derived from a
fossil fuel feedstock.
(C) Developing, constructing, or installing microgrids
and associated infrastructure. For purposes of this
subparagraph, “microgrid” means a microgrid as
defined in subdivision (d) of Section 8370 of the Public
Utilities Code.
(D) Capturing, transporting, or storing carbon dioxide
emissions for permanent isolation from sources,
including, but not limited to, energy production,
manufacturing, or refining facilities.
(E) Developing, constructing, upgrading, or expanding
transmission or distribution system components
identified in a transmission planning process approved
by the Independent System Operator or in an integrated
energy policy report adopted pursuant to Section
25302, including financing of those facilities, assets, or
components through sale, lease, assignment,
mortgage, or other disposition or encumbrance
requiring state agency approval.
(2) An “essential clean energy project” shall comply
with all labor requirements described in Section
21183.5.
(k) (1) “Essential education facility project” means the
acquisition, construction, expansion, remodeling,
renovation, improvement, furnishing, or equipping of an
educational facility.
(2) An essential education facility project shall comply
with all labor requirements described in Section
21183.5.
(l) “Essential housing project” means all of the
following:
(1) Residential units only.
(2) A mixed-use development.
(3) Transitional housing, emergency shelters, or
supportive housing, as defined in Section 65582 of the
Government Code.
(4) Farmworker housing, as defined in subdivision (h)
of Section 50199.7 of the Health and Safety Code.

(5) Group living accommodations, meaning buildings
or portion of any buildings designed for or
accommodating a residential use by persons not living
together as a household, typically without separate

residential units or group living accommodation
intended for use by students, including, without

(7) (A) Senior housing units. For purposes of this

(B) This paragraph shall not be construed to limit the

(8) A subdivision or common interest development, as
defined in Section 4100 of the Civil Code, consisting of

(9) A conversion of an existing commercial building to
residential use.
(m) “Essential project” means a project that meets all

(1) (A) The project is an essential housing project,

(2) The project does not include a jail or other detention

(2) An “essential public health project” shall comply
with all labor requirements described in Section
21183.5.
(o) (1) “Essential public safety project” means a first

(2) (A) An “essential public safety project” shall

(B) A wildfire risk reduction project limited to

assistantMessageEvent.content:
The Lookout article requires registration. Not crucial.

Key text findings confirmed:
- Judicial review: substantial evidence standard for challenges; remedies limited to prohibiting commencement of noncomplying part; courts may not rescind approval; injunctive relief only on clear and convincing evidence of specific adverse public safety impact.
- Administrative record limited to documents distributed publicly and specified comments; late comments excluded.
- 270-day deadline including trial and appeal; only 90-day extension at court's discretion, otherwise requires mutual consent.
- "Consulting tribe" = federally recognized only; this replaces "California Native American tribe" in key CEQA tribal cultural resources sections — a real reduction in tribal rights, confirmed by LA Times reporting.
- "Essential housing project" includes subdivisions of unimproved residential lots — i.e., greenfield sprawl housing.
- "Essential project" includes all related and ancillary public/private/utility infrastructure.
- "Existing laws" = those in effect when application submitted (vested rights freeze), with narrow life-safety exception.
- Clean energy includes carbon capture, hydrogen, transmission/distribution upgrades.
- Transportation includes Article XIX projects (highways, roads) — so freeway expansions.
- Labor: prevailing wage requirements (Section 21183.5) apply to non-housing essential projects; housing only for buildings over 85 feet.

Let me now check the last chunk of the text (offset 80000) for Section 21029 (interpretation) and the amendment clause (2/3) and severability. Also the alternatives analysis provision (probably around offset 40000). Let me fetch offset 80000 and offset 40000.

Then I'll consider the final decision.

Actually, let me also weigh: is there any credible analysis arguing that Prop 45's substantive changes are overstated? The Yes campaign and Sean Marciniak argue agencies retain discretion to approve/deny, prevailing wage and tribal protections preserved, deadlines enforceable both ways. Also the Legislative Counsel opinion on broadband definition (though about net neutrality law). The East Bay Times/Mercury News editorial board (majority) said yes; Santa Cruz Sentinel said yes (majority of editorial board). 26 newspapers + WSJ endorsed yes. SF Chronicle said no; Press Democrat (Sonoma) said no.

Let me check the balance of editorial endorsements more comprehensively — cityhallpass.com had a list. Also check the LA Times editorial board (did they eventually endorse?). Let me search.

## The basics
Proposition 45 would impose stricter deadlines on environmental reviews, permits and court challenges.
Agencies would have to spell out application requirements up-front and could not make repeated requests for more information or project changes.
The measure caps public comment periods, while current law only sets minimum lengths.
It also limits what courts may consider in CEQA lawsuits.
## The impact
The law clearly would change the CEQA process; whether that would be for better or worse is the subject of debate.
Backers say it would make the process faster and easier.
Critics say it would roll back important environmental protections.

approval of essential projects, as defined in this act,

## The basics
Proposition 45 would impose stricter deadlines on environmental reviews, permits and court challenges.
Agencies would have to spell out application requirements up-front and could not make repeated requests for more information or project changes.
The measure caps public comment periods, while current law only sets minimum lengths.
It also limits what courts may consider in CEQA lawsuits.

The law clearly would change the CEQA process; whether that would be for better or worse is the subject of debate.
Backers say it would make the process faster and easier.
Critics say it would roll back important environmental protections.

In the event that this initiative measure and another
measure or measures pertaining to the review or
approval of essential projects, as defined in this act,
shall appear on the same statewide election ballot, the
other measure or measures shall be deemed to be in
conflict with this measure. In the event that this
initiative measure receives a greater number of

prevail in their entirety, and the provisions of the other

This act shall be liberally construed to give effect to its

The purpose of this section is to ensure that the

## The basics
Proposition 45 would impose stricter deadlines on environmental reviews, permits and court challenges.
Agencies would have to spell out application requirements up-front and could not make repeated requests for more information or project changes.
The measure caps public comment periods, while current law only sets minimum lengths.
It also limits what courts may consider in CEQA lawsuits.
## The impact
The law clearly would change the CEQA process; whether that would be for better or worse is the subject of debate.
Backers say it would make the process faster and easier.
Critics say it would roll back important environmental protections.

Let me weigh the considerations:

Considerations favoring YES:
- Genuine, documented problem: CEQA abuse/delay raises costs of housing and public infrastructure; litigation risk is used strategically (NIMBY, labor leverage).

- Optional: agencies/applicants can choose; agencies retain approval/disapproval authority; prevailing wage requirements largely preserved.

Weighing: The core issue is whether the expected benefits (faster/cheaper building) outweigh the expected costs (weakened, locked-in environmental/community protections with high uncertainty, plus a one-way ratchet that prevents legislative correction). Given:
1. The measure is a 41-page initiative with sweeping provisions beyond deadlines, including field preemption and frozen cross-references, amendable only by 2/3;
2. The most acute problem (housing delay) was already addressed legislatively in 2025 with measurable success;
3. Independent legal experts broadly agree it goes too far and creates uncertainty (the SF Chronicle editorial board — no; Press Democrat — no; LA Times Skelton — no);
4. It weakens tribal consultation and community input in ways that are hard to justify;
5. Costs: up to $100M+/yr near-term;
6. There remains a viable legislative path for targeted, amendable reform (and Newsom/Becerra are actively pushing permitting reform),

I'd conclude "no" is the better choice. The irreversibility (2/3 lock-in, no sunset, frozen references, field occupation) is decisive: a risky, poorly-drafted, interest-group-written rewrite of the state's foundational environmental law that can't be fixed by a majority vote is a bad bet, especially when targeted reform is already working and can continue through the Legislature.

But let me steelman "yes" once more before finalizing. Consider that:
- CEQA delays are a real driver of California's cost crisis; waiting for the Legislature has produced decades of piecemeal carve-outs with strings attached (as the East Bay Times argued). A "no" may just perpetuate the status quo.
- The measure keeps environmental review; it does not exempt projects; standards still apply; agencies can still deny; courts can still order corrections.
- Many of the critics' worst readings (data centers, permanent regulatory freeze, repeal of CEQA) are contested by the drafters and some attorneys; courts would construe reasonably.
- The 270-day court deadline and 365-day EIR deadline mirror existing "environmental leadership" streamlining (CEQA §21185) that has been used for major projects.

However, the "contested interpretations" point cuts both ways: with a 2/3 amendment lock, uncertainty is costly and unfixable. And several provisions are not ambiguous on their face: the tribal narrowing (explicit), the 45-day comment cap and record exclusion (explicit), the remedy limits (explicit), the vested-rights freeze (explicit), the field occupation (explicit), the frozen statutory references (explicit). Those are textually clear reductions in protection, not just campaign scare claims.

Meanwhile the benefits are uncertain (no affordability requirement; housing largely already exempt; savings estimates from an interested party's study).

Weighing expected value: asymmetric risk. A "no" keeps a functioning (if slow) system and preserves legislative flexibility to enact targeted reform; a "yes" installs a hard-to-reverse, interest-drafted regime with substantial downside for environment, EJ communities, and tribes, and speculative upside on costs.

So: no.

Let me do a couple more checks to be fair — specifically, whether there's evidence that the deadlines alone would meaningfully reduce housing costs, and whether the "no" side is mainly labor protecting leverage. Also let me check the outcome of the actual election? Today is Nov 3, 2026 (election day) — results not in. I shouldn't rely on results anyway.

content.thinking:
Important text findings from the last chunk:
- Section 21029: courts should not interpret CEQA to impose requirements beyond those explicitly stated; constrains courts' authority to issue remedies not expressly authorized. Combined with "fullest possible weight to... approval and realization of essential projects."
- Section 21030: declares the state "occupies the field" in review/approval of essential projects — preempting local ordinances that are stricter? This is a big deal for local control (contradicting claims that local control is preserved). Actually "occupies the field in the area of review and approval of essential projects as provided in this chapter" — meaning local rules about review/approval processes are preempted.
- Section 21031: all statutory references frozen as of Dec 31, 2025 regardless of subsequent amendment/repeal/sunset. This means future legislative reforms to CEQA or other laws referenced would not apply to essential projects — a big lock-in. E.g., if the Legislature later strengthens protections (like SB 954-type), essential projects would still be governed by Dec 31, 2025 versions. That's a serious concern: it prevents the Legislature from improving environmental protections for covered projects even with a simple majority... well, they could amend this chapter by 2/3 only. Hmm, but a new statute that changes referenced laws might be argued to conflict with this chapter and thus require 2/3. This is the "one-way ratchet."
- Section 21032 severability; Section 21034 amendments require 2/3 and must further purposes; SEC 4 mandates independent counsel and continuous General Fund appropriation to defend the act.

This confirms the lock-in critique and the field-occupation preemption of local review rules.

Now, on the other side, note the labor standards preserved (21183.5 prevailing wage) for most categories, and housing prevailing wage only over 85 feet. Also tribal consultation with federally recognized tribes is maintained with confidentiality protections.

Now, decision analysis. The question: "Is it better to vote yes or no on this prop?" I need to answer with only `yes` or `no`.

Let me weigh the considerations:

Considerations favoring YES:
- Genuine, documented problem: CEQA abuse/delay raises costs of housing and public infrastructure; litigation risk is used strategically (NIMBY, labor leverage).
- Deadlines with enforceability are a reasonable reform; many other states/federal permitting reforms do similar (federal BAAJA-type reform; NEPA one-year EIS goals).
- Broad, diverse coalition support: hospitals, water agencies, affordable housing council, clean energy (Large-Scale Solar Association, American Clean Power), Farm Bureau, LULAC, Hispanic chambers, building trades? no. Editorial boards mostly yes (26 papers + WSJ).
- Cost savings: $75k/home claim (from BIA), Blue Sky Consulting study claims $1.5B in savings/revenue for public agencies.
- Optional: agencies/applicants can choose; agencies retain approval/disapproval authority; prevailing wage requirements largely preserved.
- Status quo alternative is not great: the Legislature has been unable/unwilling to do comprehensive reform; Newsom vetoed SB 954 (narrowing manufacturing exemptions) — showing the direction of travel is toward streamlining.

Considerations favoring NO:
- Scope far exceeds streamlining: rewrites substantive CEQA (single alternative proposed by applicant; freeze of standards at application date; narrowed record; limits on remedies; preclusion of subsequent challenges; "fullest possible weight" to approval; occupies the field; frozen statutory references as of Dec 31, 2025).
- Lock-in: 2/3 to amend and only to further purposes; no sunset; frozen cross-references → hard/impossible to fix errors, and blocks future legislative strengthening of protections for covered projects.
- Breadth of covered projects: greenfield subdivisions, freeway expansions, logging/vegetation management, dams/irrigation, carbon capture, transmission, possibly data centers via "ancillary infrastructure" — with the biggest environmental impacts.
- Equity: caps public comment at 45 days, excludes late comments from record, narrows judicial review → less community leverage, especially for EJ communities; tribal consultation limited to federally recognized tribes, excluding many California tribes (a significant, hard-to-defend provision).
- Housing already addressed: AB 130/SB 131 (2025) exempt most infill housing and are producing results (~18k units in 15 months). Prop 45's marginal housing benefit is small relative to its breadth. YIMBY flagships (California YIMBY, YIMBY Action, SPUR, Abundant Housing LA) declined to endorse; Greenbelt Alliance and EastBay for Everyone oppose; Scott Wiener neutral; Tom Steyer opposes.
- Fiscal: LAO projects initial costs up to >$100M/yr; uncertain long-term; savings claims come from a Chamber-commissioned study.
- Money/interest alignment: Yes funded by builders ($10.5M BIA), tech ($10M Building a Better California), utilities (PG&E $2.3M, Edison $2M), oil producer CRC ($1M total), data center builders ($2M from three).
- Timing: federal rollback of ESA/NEPA under Trump makes state CEQA a more critical backstop.
- Expert consensus among independent legal scholars (Berkeley's Biber, UCLA's Stein, Loyola's Selmi, UC Davis's Frank, Stanford's Sivas) is that it goes well beyond streamlining and creates significant uncertainty; the nonpartisan LAO's analysis lists substantive changes; even historically pro-reform rural counties stayed neutral with a policy advocate calling it "too far."

Weighing: The core issue is whether the expected benefits (faster/cheaper building) outweigh the expected costs (weakened, locked-in environmental/community protections with high uncertainty, plus a one-way ratchet that prevents legislative correction). Given:
1. The measure is a 41-page initiative with sweeping provisions beyond deadlines, including field preemption and frozen cross-references, amendable only by 2/3;
2. The most acute problem (housing delay) was already addressed legislatively in 2025 with measurable success;
3. Independent legal experts broadly agree it goes too far and creates uncertainty (the SF Chronicle editorial board — no; Press Democrat — no; LA Times Skelton — no);
4. It weakens tribal consultation and community input in ways that are hard to justify;
5. Costs: up to $100M+/yr near-term;
