SDtaxpayers.org • 1
Building an Affordable California Act
August 2026
TAXPAYERS ASSOCIATION POSITION SUPPORT
Rationale for Position:
Proposition 45 directly targets the kind of cost-and-delay driver relevant to the public projects
the Association reviews — open-ended CEQA review and litigation timelines — by replacing
them with enforceable deadlines, objective standards, and a proportionate “fix-it” remedy, while
leaving substantive environmental standards, local agencies’ approval authority, and prevailing-
wage/skilled-workforce labor standards in place. Because nearly half of all CEQA lawsuits target
taxpayer-funded projects with no private sponsor, the delay and legal-defense costs the measure
addresses fall disproportionately on public budgets. The nonpartisan LAO concludes the measure
would likely produce net savings for state and local governments over the long term and could
increase state and local tax revenue through faster project completion.
Title: Proposition 45, Building an Affordable California Act (Affordable CA). Official ballot
title: “Modifies environmental review for certain projects.”
Type: Statewide Statutory Initiative
Vote: November 2026 Statewide General Election
Status: Qualified for the November 2026 ballot by the California Secretary of State on June
16, 2026, after exceeding the 601,317-signature random-sample threshold (546,651 valid
signatures required).
Description: Reform of the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) review and
permitting process for designated essential projects.
Fiscal Impact: Legislative Analyst’s Office official fiscal impact statement issued at
qualification (June 2026): “State and local government implementation costs in the tens of
millions of dollars annually for the first several years. Over the long term, the annual net fiscal
effects are uncertain, but state and local governments likely would experience net savings due
to reduced administrative and legal workload. Net fiscal effects on state trial courts ranging
from annual savings of up to the tens of millions of dollars to annual costs of up to the low tens
of millions of dollars.”
Background
The California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) is a state law enacted in 1970 which requires
local and state public agencies to assess and publicly disclose the environmental impacts of
proposed land development projects, and develop mitigation measures for those impacts in order
to secure project approval. The basic goal of CEQA is to prevent undue damage to the
SDtaxpayers.org • 2
environment and ensure the general public is informed in cases where there will be impacts to
the environment, while providing opportunities for the public to raise concerns and provide input
on such projects. It applies to all public projects as well as any private projects which require
government approval. CEQA review can take the form of a categorical exemption, a negative
declaration or mitigated negative declaration (ND/MND), or a full environmental impact report
(EIR), depending on a project’s potential effects. CEQA also allows members of the public to
challenge an agency’s approval in court.
Proponents of the Building an Affordable California Act (BACA) contend that the current
process imposes open-ended delay that raises the cost of housing, water, energy, transportation,
health care, and wildfire-resilience projects, and that those costs are ultimately borne by renters,
homebuyers, ratepayers, and taxpayers. The sponsor estimates that permitting and approval
delays add more than $75,000 to the cost of a new single-family home and billions of dollars to
the cost of public infrastructure. Independent research supports the direction of the claim if not
the precise number: an environmental impact report commonly costs from $200,000 to several
million dollars to prepare, industry analyses estimate that regulatory requirements add a wide
range—on the order of several thousand to well over one hundred thousand dollars—to the cost
of a home, and recent academic work on permitting (Soltas and Gruber, 2026) finds that
permitting requirements and delay materially raise housing costs.
Independent empirical study of CEQA litigation provides important context for the measure, and
the pattern has held across more than a decade of data. A Holland & Knight review of every
CEQA lawsuit filed statewide from 2010 through 2012 found that housing, particularly higher-
density infill housing, is the most frequently litigated category of private project, that transit is
the most frequently litigated category of infrastructure, that 49 percent of CEQA lawsuits
targeted taxpayer-funded projects with no private sponsor (parks, schools, libraries, and public
housing), and that roughly two-thirds of petitioners were individuals or local associations, many
without a prior record of environmental advocacy. A more recent study in the same series,
examining litigation filed from 2019 through 2021, found that the housing focus persisted: in
2020 alone, CEQA lawsuits targeted approximately 48,000 approved housing units—close to
half of the roughly 111,000 homes California produces in an average year—with thousands more
units challenged through suits against neighborhood upzoning.
Analysts who view CEQA more favorably draw a different emphasis from overlapping data.
Studies commissioned by the Rose Foundation for Communities and the Environment report that
CEQA lawsuits have averaged roughly 192 per year since 2002 and that only about 1.9 percent
of projects reviewed under CEQA from 2013 through 2021 were litigated, and conclude that
CEQA is not a major obstacle to housing production statewide. Both perspectives bear on this
measure: CEQA litigation is statistically infrequent across the full universe of projects, yet it
falls disproportionately on the housing and taxpayer-funded projects the measure is intended to
accelerate.
SDtaxpayers.org • 3
The measure also arrives against a CEQA baseline that the Legislature changed materially in
2025. Assembly Bill 130 and Senate Bill 131, signed in June 2025, created a broad statutory
CEQA exemption for qualifying infill housing and narrowed review for projects that “near-miss”
an exemption, among other changes. The Building an Affordable California Act is the California
Chamber of Commerce’s response to what proponents view as the limits of those project-specific
fixes: a comprehensive, statewide revision of CEQA procedure rather than additional category-
by-category exemptions. Any comparison of the measure to “current CEQA” in this paper is a
comparison to the post-2025 framework, not to legacy CEQA.
The Proposal
The measure adds a new chapter to the Public Resources Code that applies streamlined CEQA
procedures to a defined set of “essential projects” including housing (single- and multi-family,
senior, student, supportive, farmworker, and commercial-to-residential conversions); health care
facilities; clean drinking water and water-system infrastructure; clean energy generation, storage,
and transmission; education facilities; public safety and wildfire-resilience projects;
transportation; and broadband. The measure does not exempt these projects from CEQA or other
environmental statutes, rather it changes the timeline and the rules of review. Its principal
mechanisms are:
● Application completeness: an agency must determine whether an application is complete
within 30 days, or the application is deemed complete automatically.
● CEQA-track selection: the agency must choose the document type (EIR, ND/MND, or
exemption) within 30 days of completeness.
● Enforceable review timelines: 365 days for an EIR, 180 days for an ND/MND, and 90 days
for an exemption or addendum. If a deadline is missed, the applicant may request a hearing at
which a decision must be made within 60 days, and may seek a writ from the court.
● Final agency decision: the agency must act within 90 days after CEQA review is complete,
and all responsible agencies must act within their own deadlines.
● Narrowed alternatives analysis: an EIR needs to analyze only one feasible alternative
design that reduces environmental impacts plus a “no project” alternative.
● Judicial “shot clock”: courts must resolve a legal challenge within 270 days.
● Standard of review: a court may overturn an approval only where the agency ignored
objective written standards in effect when the application was submitted, and must uphold an
approval supported by substantial evidence—a more deferential standard than the “fair
argument” and “prejudicial abuse of discretion” standards applied under current law.
● Severance (“fix-it ticket”) remedy: where one portion of a review document is found
deficient, only that portion must be corrected and the approval is not rescinded, allowing the
remainder of the project to proceed.
SDtaxpayers.org • 4
● Legal-defense provision: if the Act is challenged in court and both the Governor and
Attorney General decline to defend it, the measure requires the Attorney General to appoint
independent counsel to defend the Act and creates a continuous appropriation from the
General Fund, without regard to fiscal year, to cover that defense.
● Conflicting-measures clause: if another measure concerning the review or approval of
essential projects appears on the same statewide ballot, the two are deemed in conflict, and if
this measure receives more affirmative votes, its provisions prevail in their entirety and the
other measure’s conflicting provisions become null and void. Staff is not aware of a currently
qualified competing measure this clause would apply against.
The sponsor states that the measure preserves local agencies’ authority to approve or deny
projects, retains a public-comment period, strengthens early tribal consultation, and requires
prevailing-wage and skilled-and-trained workforce labor standards.
Fiscal Impact
The measure is not a tax and dedicates no revenue. Its fiscal relevance to taxpayers is indirect but
material: governments are themselves major builders of the essential projects the measure
covers—water systems, roads and bridges, schools, fire stations, and energy infrastructure—and
review delay adds financing, legal, labor, and materials cost to those public projects. The
taxpayer exposure is not merely theoretical. The Holland & Knight litigation study found that
nearly half of all CEQA lawsuits target taxpayer-funded projects with no private sponsor, and
that transit is the most-litigated category of infrastructure; for those projects, the cost of delay
and of defending the litigation falls directly on public budgets. More predictable timelines and a
narrower set of litigable issues would be expected to reduce both the carrying cost and the legal-
defense cost of public capital projects.
The strongest independent support for the measure’s fiscal case comes from the state’s own
analyst. The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, in its December 10, 2025 review,
concluded that the net effect of the measure’s shortened agency and court timelines “likely
result[s] in savings in the longer term,” and noted that faster project completion could increase
state and local tax revenue, such as property tax.
Governance Impact
The Taxpayers Association evaluates not only what a measure costs but how it changes the
structure of public decision-making—who decides, under what standards, with what oversight,
and answerable to whom. In its bond analyses the Association treats governance as a distinct
evaluation axis, examining board policies, oversight committees, and transparency commitments
alongside the financing. This measure is, at its core, a governance measure: it leaves the
SDtaxpayers.org • 5
substantive environmental standards in place and instead rewrites the procedural rules that
allocate authority among agencies, courts, applicants, and the public.
Under CEQA as it operates today, environmental review is enforced largely through private
litigation rather than by a dedicated regulator. Members of the public and organizations may file
suit to compel additional review, and the governing standards are claimant-friendly: for a
negative declaration, the “fair argument” standard requires an agency to prepare a full
environmental impact report whenever any substantial evidence supports a fair argument of a
significant effect—a threshold courts have described as easy to meet. A successful challenge is
typically remedied by a writ that sets aside the approval and requires the agency to redo the
deficient review, and there are no statutory deadlines governing how long agency review or the
ensuing litigation may take. This design gives the public and the courts substantial leverage over
project approvals, which is its intended virtue and, proponents argue, the source of its cost and
delay.
The measure rebalances that structure toward agencies and applicants. It directs courts to review
approvals for substantial evidence rather than under the more searching fair-argument and
independent-judgment standards, which makes a compliant approval harder to overturn. It
restricts the issues that may be litigated to an agency’s departure from objective written standards
in effect when the application was filed, and bars “late” objections not raised during the
comment period. It replaces the set-aside-and-redo remedy with a severance or “fix-it” remedy,
so that a single defective portion of a review document is corrected without rescinding the whole
approval. And it imposes enforceable deadlines on both agencies (365 days for an EIR, 180 for a
negative declaration, 90 for an exemption, and 90 days for a final decision) and courts (270 days
to resolve a challenge). The net effect is a more predictable, schedule-driven process in which
the decisive judgment rests with the permitting agency rather than with a reviewing court or a
litigant.
The accountability the measure adds is real and of a kind the Association generally favors:
objective standards known in advance, firm timelines, and a defined remedy for missed deadlines
replace open-ended, discretionary delay with rules a public can hold agencies to. At the same

challenge an agency’s approval in court.

process imposes open-ended delay that raises the cost of housing, water, energy, transportation,
health care, and wildfire-resilience projects, and that those costs are ultimately borne by renters,
homebuyers, ratepayers, and taxpayers. The sponsor estimates that permitting and approval
delays add more than $75,000 to the cost of a new single-family home and billions of dollars to

the precise number: an environmental impact report commonly costs from $200,000 to several
million dollars to prepare, industry analyses estimate that regulatory requirements add a wide
range—on the order of several thousand to well over one hundred thousand dollars—to the cost
of a home, and recent academic work on permitting (Soltas and Gruber, 2026) finds that
permitting requirements and delay materially raise housing costs.

the pattern has held across more than a decade of data. A Holland & Knight review of every

density infill housing, is the most frequently litigated category of private project, that transit is
the most frequently litigated category of infrastructure, that 49 percent of CEQA lawsuits
targeted taxpayer-funded projects with no private sponsor (parks, schools, libraries, and public
housing), and that roughly two-thirds of petitioners were individuals or local associations, many
without a prior record of environmental advocacy. A more recent study in the same series,

2020 alone, CEQA lawsuits targeted approximately 48,000 approved housing units—close to

The measure adds a new chapter to the Public Resources Code that applies streamlined CEQA
procedures to a defined set of “essential projects” including housing (single- and multi-family,
senior, student, supportive, farmworker, and commercial-to-residential conversions); health care

transportation; and broadband. The measure does not exempt these projects from CEQA or other
environmental statutes, rather it changes the timeline and the rules of review. Its principal

applicant’s own design plus a “no project” option removes a tool historically used to redirect

associated with sprawl. Staff independently reviewed Greenbelt’s additional claim that the

SDtaxpayers.org • 1
Building an Affordable California Act
August 2026
TAXPAYERS ASSOCIATION POSITION SUPPORT
Rationale for Position:
Proposition 45 directly targets the kind of cost-and-delay driver relevant to the public projects
the Association reviews — open-ended CEQA review and litigation timelines — by replacing
them with enforceable deadlines, objective standards, and a proportionate “fix-it” remedy, while
leaving substantive environmental standards, local agencies’ approval authority, and prevailing-
wage/skilled-workforce labor standards in place. Because nearly half of all CEQA lawsuits target
taxpayer-funded projects with no private sponsor, the delay and legal-defense costs the measure
addresses fall disproportionately on public budgets. The nonpartisan LAO concludes the measure
would likely produce net savings for state and local governments over the long term and could
increase state and local tax revenue through faster project completion.
Title: Proposition 45, Building an Affordable California Act (Affordable CA). Official ballot
title: “Modifies environmental review for certain projects.”
Type: Statewide Statutory Initiative
Vote: November 2026 Statewide General Election
Status: Qualified for the November 2026 ballot by the California Secretary of State on June
16, 2026, after exceeding the 601,317-signature random-sample threshold (546,651 valid
signatures required).
Description: Reform of the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) review and
permitting process for designated essential projects.
Fiscal Impact: Legislative Analyst’s Office official fiscal impact statement issued at
qualification (June 2026): “State and local government implementation costs in the tens of
millions of dollars annually for the first several years. Over the long term, the annual net fiscal
effects are uncertain, but state and local governments likely would experience net savings due
to reduced administrative and legal workload. Net fiscal effects on state trial courts ranging
from annual savings of up to the tens of millions of dollars to annual costs of up to the low tens
of millions of dollars.”
Background
The California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) is a state law enacted in 1970 which requires
local and state public agencies to assess and publicly disclose the environmental impacts of
proposed land development projects, and develop mitigation measures for those impacts in order
to secure project approval. The basic goal of CEQA is to prevent undue damage to the
SDtaxpayers.org • 2
environment and ensure the general public is informed in cases where there will be impacts to
the environment, while providing opportunities for the public to raise concerns and provide input
on such projects. It applies to all public projects as well as any private projects which require
government approval. CEQA review can take the form of a categorical exemption, a negative
declaration or mitigated negative declaration (ND/MND), or a full environmental impact report
(EIR), depending on a project’s potential effects. CEQA also allows members of the public to
challenge an agency’s approval in court.
Proponents of the Building an Affordable California Act (BACA) contend that the current
process imposes open-ended delay that raises the cost of housing, water, energy, transportation,
health care, and wildfire-resilience projects, and that those costs are ultimately borne by renters,
homebuyers, ratepayers, and taxpayers. The sponsor estimates that permitting and approval
delays add more than $75,000 to the cost of a new single-family home and billions of dollars to
the cost of public infrastructure. Independent research supports the direction of the claim if not
the precise number: an environmental impact report commonly costs from $200,000 to several
million dollars to prepare, industry analyses estimate that regulatory requirements add a wide
range—on the order of several thousand to well over one hundred thousand dollars—to the cost
of a home, and recent academic work on permitting (Soltas and Gruber, 2026) finds that
permitting requirements and delay materially raise housing costs.
Independent empirical study of CEQA litigation provides important context for the measure, and
the pattern has held across more than a decade of data. A Holland & Knight review of every
CEQA lawsuit filed statewide from 2010 through 2012 found that housing, particularly higher-
density infill housing, is the most frequently litigated category of private project, that transit is
the most frequently litigated category of infrastructure, that 49 percent of CEQA lawsuits
targeted taxpayer-funded projects with no private sponsor (parks, schools, libraries, and public
housing), and that roughly two-thirds of petitioners were individuals or local associations, many
without a prior record of environmental advocacy. A more recent study in the same series,
examining litigation filed from 2019 through 2021, found that the housing focus persisted: in
2020 alone, CEQA lawsuits targeted approximately 48,000 approved housing units—close to
half of the roughly 111,000 homes California produces in an average year—with thousands more
units challenged through suits against neighborhood upzoning.
Analysts who view CEQA more favorably draw a different emphasis from overlapping data.
Studies commissioned by the Rose Foundation for Communities and the Environment report that
CEQA lawsuits have averaged roughly 192 per year since 2002 and that only about 1.9 percent
of projects reviewed under CEQA from 2013 through 2021 were litigated, and conclude that
CEQA is not a major obstacle to housing production statewide. Both perspectives bear on this
measure: CEQA litigation is statistically infrequent across the full universe of projects, yet it
falls disproportionately on the housing and taxpayer-funded projects the measure is intended to
accelerate.
SDtaxpayers.org • 3
The measure also arrives against a CEQA baseline that the Legislature changed materially in
2025. Assembly Bill 130 and Senate Bill 131, signed in June 2025, created a broad statutory
CEQA exemption for qualifying infill housing and narrowed review for projects that “near-miss”
an exemption, among other changes. The Building an Affordable California Act is the California
Chamber of Commerce’s response to what proponents view as the limits of those project-specific
fixes: a comprehensive, statewide revision of CEQA procedure rather than additional category-
by-category exemptions. Any comparison of the measure to “current CEQA” in this paper is a
comparison to the post-2025 framework, not to legacy CEQA.
The Proposal
The measure adds a new chapter to the Public Resources Code that applies streamlined CEQA
procedures to a defined set of “essential projects” including housing (single- and multi-family,
senior, student, supportive, farmworker, and commercial-to-residential conversions); health care
facilities; clean drinking water and water-system infrastructure; clean energy generation, storage,
and transmission; education facilities; public safety and wildfire-resilience projects;
transportation; and broadband. The measure does not exempt these projects from CEQA or other
environmental statutes, rather it changes the timeline and the rules of review. Its principal
mechanisms are:
● Application completeness: an agency must determine whether an application is complete
within 30 days, or the application is deemed complete automatically.
● CEQA-track selection: the agency must choose the document type (EIR, ND/MND, or
exemption) within 30 days of completeness.
● Enforceable review timelines: 365 days for an EIR, 180 days for an ND/MND, and 90 days
for an exemption or addendum. If a deadline is missed, the applicant may request a hearing at
which a decision must be made within 60 days, and may seek a writ from the court.
● Final agency decision: the agency must act within 90 days after CEQA review is complete,
and all responsible agencies must act within their own deadlines.
● Narrowed alternatives analysis: an EIR needs to analyze only one feasible alternative
design that reduces environmental impacts plus a “no project” alternative.
● Judicial “shot clock”: courts must resolve a legal challenge within 270 days.
● Standard of review: a court may overturn an approval only where the agency ignored
objective written standards in effect when the application was submitted, and must uphold an
approval supported by substantial evidence—a more deferential standard than the “fair
argument” and “prejudicial abuse of discretion” standards applied under current law.
● Severance (“fix-it ticket”) remedy: where one portion of a review document is found
deficient, only that portion must be corrected and the approval is not rescinded, allowing the
remainder of the project to proceed.
SDtaxpayers.org • 4
● Legal-defense provision: if the Act is challenged in court and both the Governor and
Attorney General decline to defend it, the measure requires the Attorney General to appoint
independent counsel to defend the Act and creates a continuous appropriation from the
General Fund, without regard to fiscal year, to cover that defense.
● Conflicting-measures clause: if another measure concerning the review or approval of
essential projects appears on the same statewide ballot, the two are deemed in conflict, and if
this measure receives more affirmative votes, its provisions prevail in their entirety and the
other measure’s conflicting provisions become null and void. Staff is not aware of a currently
qualified competing measure this clause would apply against.
The sponsor states that the measure preserves local agencies’ authority to approve or deny
projects, retains a public-comment period, strengthens early tribal consultation, and requires
prevailing-wage and skilled-and-trained workforce labor standards.
Fiscal Impact
The measure is not a tax and dedicates no revenue. Its fiscal relevance to taxpayers is indirect but
material: governments are themselves major builders of the essential projects the measure
covers—water systems, roads and bridges, schools, fire stations, and energy infrastructure—and
review delay adds financing, legal, labor, and materials cost to those public projects. The
taxpayer exposure is not merely theoretical. The Holland & Knight litigation study found that
nearly half of all CEQA lawsuits target taxpayer-funded projects with no private sponsor, and
that transit is the most-litigated category of infrastructure; for those projects, the cost of delay
and of defending the litigation falls directly on public budgets. More predictable timelines and a
narrower set of litigable issues would be expected to reduce both the carrying cost and the legal-
defense cost of public capital projects.
The strongest independent support for the measure’s fiscal case comes from the state’s own
analyst. The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, in its December 10, 2025 review,
concluded that the net effect of the measure’s shortened agency and court timelines “likely
result[s] in savings in the longer term,” and noted that faster project completion could increase
state and local tax revenue, such as property tax.
Governance Impact
The Taxpayers Association evaluates not only what a measure costs but how it changes the
structure of public decision-making—who decides, under what standards, with what oversight,
and answerable to whom. In its bond analyses the Association treats governance as a distinct
evaluation axis, examining board policies, oversight committees, and transparency commitments
alongside the financing. This measure is, at its core, a governance measure: it leaves the
SDtaxpayers.org • 5
substantive environmental standards in place and instead rewrites the procedural rules that
allocate authority among agencies, courts, applicants, and the public.
Under CEQA as it operates today, environmental review is enforced largely through private
litigation rather than by a dedicated regulator. Members of the public and organizations may file
suit to compel additional review, and the governing standards are claimant-friendly: for a
negative declaration, the “fair argument” standard requires an agency to prepare a full
environmental impact report whenever any substantial evidence supports a fair argument of a
significant effect—a threshold courts have described as easy to meet. A successful challenge is
typically remedied by a writ that sets aside the approval and requires the agency to redo the
deficient review, and there are no statutory deadlines governing how long agency review or the
ensuing litigation may take. This design gives the public and the courts substantial leverage over
project approvals, which is its intended virtue and, proponents argue, the source of its cost and
delay.
The measure rebalances that structure toward agencies and applicants. It directs courts to review
approvals for substantial evidence rather than under the more searching fair-argument and
independent-judgment standards, which makes a compliant approval harder to overturn. It
restricts the issues that may be litigated to an agency’s departure from objective written standards
in effect when the application was filed, and bars “late” objections not raised during the
comment period. It replaces the set-aside-and-redo remedy with a severance or “fix-it” remedy,
so that a single defective portion of a review document is corrected without rescinding the whole
approval. And it imposes enforceable deadlines on both agencies (365 days for an EIR, 180 for a
negative declaration, 90 for an exemption, and 90 days for a final decision) and courts (270 days
to resolve a challenge). The net effect is a more predictable, schedule-driven process in which
the decisive judgment rests with the permitting agency rather than with a reviewing court or a
litigant.
The accountability the measure adds is real and of a kind the Association generally favors:
objective standards known in advance, firm timelines, and a defined remedy for missed deadlines
replace open-ended, discretionary delay with rules a public can hold agencies to. At the same
time, the measure reduces a different form of accountability—the public’s and the courts’ ability
to force a fuller second look at a project—and concentrates more authority in the approving
agency. This trade is the central governance question the measure poses, and it is distinct from
the 2025 reforms (AB 130 and SB 131), which mostly exempted defined categories of infill
housing from review; this measure instead changes the standards and remedies that apply when
review and litigation do occur, across a far broader set of essential projects.
Proponents
The measure is sponsored by the California Chamber of Commerce through the Committee to
Build an Affordable California. The sponsor reports a coalition of more than 100 organizations,
including business and taxpayer groups (California Business Roundtable, Bay Area Council,
SDtaxpayers.org • 6
numerous regional chambers, and peer taxpayer associations), affordable-housing organizations
(California Council for Affordable Housing, Housing Action Coalition, Leading Builders of
America), clean-energy and water interests (American Clean Power California, California
Energy Storage Alliance, California Water Association), the California Hospital Association,
building and construction trades and contractors, and several civil-rights and community
organizations (CA/HI State Conference NAACP, LULAC). Proponents argue that decades of
project-specific fixes have failed to address the underlying cost of delay and that a
comprehensive, enforceable timeline is needed to lower the cost of housing, energy, water, and
health care while keeping California’s environmental and labor standards in place.
Opponents
Opposition is led by environmental, public-health, and conservation organizations, including
Sierra Club California, Greenbelt Alliance, the Planning and Conservation League, the Center
for Biological Diversity, Communities for a Better Environment, Food & Water Watch, and
Physicians for Social Responsibility–Los Angeles. Opponents argue that the measure weakens
environmental review by compressing timelines and limiting the grounds and remedies for legal
challenges; that the more deferential substantial- evidence standard and the bar on rescinding
approvals make it harder for courts to halt harmful projects; that the costs of pollution and
public-health impacts would shift onto taxpayers and local governments; and that reduced review
could affect air and water quality and communities near industrial projects.
Greenbelt Alliance has published a more detailed critique making several additional points: that
the measure’s definition of “essential projects” is broad enough to cover freeways, freeway
expansions, and large-scale sprawl development rather than only the infill housing the sponsor
emphasizes; that compressing review to fixed timelines is unworkable for large projects
requiring extensive species and habitat surveys; that limiting the alternatives analysis to the
applicant’s own design plus a “no project” option removes a tool historically used to redirect
development away from sensitive land; and that the measure may be cheaper to build under but
more costly to sustain over time, given the long-run infrastructure and maintenance costs
associated with sprawl. Staff independently reviewed Greenbelt’s additional claim that the
measure imposes a two-thirds legislative-supermajority requirement on future amendment and
found no such provision in the qualified initiative text; the measure contains no amendment
section at all, meaning the default rule under Article II, Section 10(c) of the California
Constitution would apply instead, under which the Legislature may not amend or repeal the Act
without a subsequent vote of the people unless the Act itself provides otherwise.

assistantMessageEvent.content:
This is a very useful independent analysis (San Diego County Taxpayers Association, position: SUPPORT).

Note the discrepancy: this August 2026 analysis says the qualified initiative text has no amendment section, meaning the default rule applies — the Legislature could not amend or repeal without a vote of the people at all (even stricter!). But the final ballot text (Section 21034) includes a 2/3 amendment provision if consistent with and furthering purposes. Either way, it's a strong lock-in. Actually the final text's 2/3 amendment clause is more permissive than the constitutional default, but still very restrictive (and only in furtherance of purposes — a one-way ratchet).

Also note: LAO's December 2025 fiscal estimate (at qualification) said "state and local governments likely would experience net savings" long-term — but the final VIG estimate says "uncertain, but potentially more significant positive or negative fiscal effects" with initial costs possibly >$100M annually. So the LAO revised its estimate downward/more uncertain after the final text.

Key mechanisms per SD Taxpayers:
- Application completeness deemed after 30 days
- 365 days EIR, 180 ND/MND, 90 exemption
- Narrowed alternatives: only one feasible alternative + no project
- 270-day judicial shot clock
- Standard of review: court may overturn only where agency ignored objective written standards in effect at application; substantial evidence deferential standard
- Severance remedy ("fix-it ticket")
- Bars late objections

That's an accurate summary of significant changes beyond timelines.

Now, my judgment. Let me think about this as a policy evaluation with expected consequences.

Arguments that this is net beneficial:
1. California's building cost/time problem is severe and well-documented (RAND: 2.5x Texas; Soltas & Gruber: permitting explains 1/3 of gap between home prices and construction costs in LA; permitting adds ~36% to construction cost). Reducing permitting friction has real, large economic benefits.
2. Nearly half of CEQA suits target taxpayer-funded public projects, so delays cost taxpayers directly.
3. Enforceable deadlines are a proven mechanism (federal FAST-41, state environmental leadership streamlining).
4. Substantive environmental laws remain (Clean Air/Water Acts, Coastal Act, ESA at federal level, state standards); agencies retain approval/denial authority; prevailing wage preserved for most categories.
5. The measure is optional for applicants.
6. Broad, diverse coalition; 26 newspaper endorsements; bipartisan (state GOP yes; some Dems like Buffy Wicks yes).

Arguments that this is net harmful:
1. It goes well beyond deadlines: it changes substantive review standards (single alternative, standards frozen at application date, deferential judicial review limited to objective written standards, severance-only remedy, exclusion of late comments, narrowed record, field preemption, frozen statutory cross-references as of Dec 31, 2025).
2. It cannot be fixed: 2/3 legislative vote and only "to further its purposes"; no sunset; frozen cross-references mean future environmental laws wouldn't apply to covered projects; plus a built-in continuous appropriation to defend it in court against the state's own elected officials.
3. Breadth: covers greenfield subdivisions, freeway expansions, logging, dams/irrigation, carbon capture, transmission, broadband/ancillary infrastructure (data centers disputed), warehouses as ancillary to housing? It reaches far beyond the housing problem the Legislature already addressed with AB 130/SB 131 (which is producing ~18k units in 15 months).
4. Equity/democracy: caps public comment at 45 days, excludes late comments from the judicial record, narrows tribes' consultation rights to federally recognized tribes (excluding most California tribes), weakens judicial remedies — reducing the main leverage EJ communities have.
5. Context: federal rollbacks under Trump (ESA habitat regs, NEPA) make state CEQA a more important backstop; locking it in weakened form now is risky.
6. Fiscal: LAO's final estimate says initial costs high tens of millions to >$100M annually; long-term effects uncertain and could be negative if harmful projects are approved.
7. Money: funded by builders, tech billionaires, utilities, an oil company, and data center developers — direct beneficiaries. Meanwhile, the pro-housing YIMBY movement's flagship organizations declined to endorse, and Greenbelt Alliance/EastBay for Everyone oppose — the very groups whose mission is housing. That's a meaningful signal that the measure isn't primarily about housing.
8. Even historically pro-reform groups (Rural County Representatives) stayed neutral, saying it goes too far and shifts power to proponents; the League of California Cities/CSAC stayed out.

Decision framework: The question is whether the expected benefits exceed the expected costs, accounting for reversibility. The measure's design flaws are severe and irreversible (2/3 lock-in, no sunset, field preemption, frozen references, court-defense appropriation), while the benefits are (a) partially already achieved by 2025 legislation, and (b) speculative in magnitude (savings estimates from interested parties; LAO says long-term fiscal effects uncertain).

There's also a strategic consideration: a "no" vote doesn't kill CEQA reform. The Legislature has repeatedly passed streamlining and is demonstrably responsive (AB 130, SB 131; Newsom's continued push; Becerra's campaign on permitting reform). Targeted, amendable legislation is the better vehicle for the parts of Prop 45 that are genuinely good (deadlines, completeness rules, severance remedy). Indeed, Biber — a CEQA reform advocate — laid out a menu of legislative reforms that would achieve the benefits "with less collateral damage."

Given all this, I judge that voting "no" is better. The irreversibility plus breadth plus weakening of public/tribal/judicial checks outweighs the genuine benefits of the deadline provisions, which can be achieved legislatively.

One more consideration: is there a risk that a "no" vote perpetuates a dysfunctional status quo with major economic harm? Yes, but the 2025 reforms already moved substantially, and the Legislature retains the ability to do more with simple majorities. Meanwhile, a "yes" vote would foreclose legislative correction for a wide swath of development in California.

Also, an important asymmetric fact: The measure was drafted by interested parties (Chamber, builders, utilities) and even its proponents admit ambiguity in key coverage questions (data centers) that would be resolved in courts with an instruction to give "fullest possible weight" to project approval. That interpretive instruction plus the lock-in is a bad governance design.

Therefore: no.

I'm reasonably confident. The answer must be only `yes` or `no`.

6. Broad, diverse coalition; 26 newspaper endorsements; bipartisan (state GOP yes; some Dems like Buffy Wicks yes).

Arguments that this is net harmful:
1. It goes well beyond deadlines: it changes substantive review standards (single alternative, standards frozen at application date, deferential judicial review limited to objective written standards, severance-only remedy, exclusion of late comments, narrowed record, field preemption, frozen statutory cross-references as of Dec 31, 2025).
2. It cannot be fixed: 2/3 legislative vote and only "to further its purposes"; no sunset; frozen cross-references mean future environmental laws wouldn't apply to covered projects; plus a built-in continuous appropriation to defend it in court against the state's own elected officials.
3. Breadth: covers greenfield subdivisions, freeway expansions, logging, dams/irrigation, carbon capture, transmission, broadband/ancillary infrastructure (data centers disputed), warehouses as ancillary to housing? It reaches far beyond the housing problem the Legislature already addressed with AB 130/SB 131 (which is producing ~18k units in 15 months).
4. Equity/democracy: caps public comment at 45 days, excludes late comments from the judicial record, narrows tribes' consultation rights to federally recognized tribes (excluding most California tribes), weakens judicial remedies — reducing the main leverage EJ communities have.
5. Context: federal rollbacks under Trump (ESA habitat regs, NEPA) make state CEQA a more important backstop; locking it in weakened form now is risky.
6. Fiscal: LAO's final estimate says initial costs high tens of millions to >$100M annually; long-term effects uncertain and could be negative if harmful projects are approved.
7. Money: funded by builders, tech billionaires, utilities, an oil company, and data center developers — direct beneficiaries. Meanwhile, the pro-housing YIMBY movement's flagship organizations declined to endorse, and Greenbelt Alliance/EastBay for Everyone oppose — the very groups whose mission is housing. That's a meaningful signal that the measure isn't primarily about housing.
8. Even historically pro-reform groups (Rural County Representatives) stayed neutral, saying it goes too far and shifts power to proponents; the League of California Cities/CSAC stayed out.

Decision framework: The question is whether the expected benefits exceed the expected costs, accounting for reversibility. The measure's design flaws are severe and irreversible (2/3 lock-in, no sunset, field preemption, frozen references, court-defense appropriation), while the benefits are (a) partially already achieved by 2025 legislation, and (b) speculative in magnitude (savings estimates from interested parties; LAO says long-term fiscal effects uncertain).

There's also a strategic consideration: a "no" vote doesn't kill CEQA reform. The Legislature has repeatedly passed streamlining and is demonstrably responsive (AB 130, SB 131; Newsom's continued push; Becerra's campaign on permitting reform). Targeted, amendable legislation is the better vehicle for the parts of Prop 45 that are genuinely good (deadlines, completeness rules, severance remedy). Indeed, Biber — a CEQA reform advocate — laid out a menu of legislative reforms that would achieve the benefits "with less collateral damage."

Given all this, I judge that voting "no" is better. The irreversibility plus breadth plus weakening of public/tribal/judicial checks outweighs the genuine benefits of the deadline provisions, which can be achieved legislatively.

One more consideration: is there a risk that a "no" vote perpetuates a dysfunctional status quo with major economic harm? Yes, but the 2025 reforms already moved substantially, and the Legislature retains the ability to do more with simple majorities. Meanwhile, a "yes" vote would foreclose legislative correction for a wide swath of development in California.

Also, an important asymmetric fact: The measure was drafted by interested parties (Chamber, builders, utilities) and even its proponents admit ambiguity in key coverage questions (data centers) that would be resolved in courts with an instruction to give "fullest possible weight" to project approval. That interpretive instruction plus the lock-in is a bad governance design.

Therefore: no.

Note the discrepancy: this August 2026 analysis says the qualified initiative text has no amendment section, meaning the default rule applies — the Legislature could not amend or repeal without a vote of the people at all (even stricter!). So the LAO revised its estimate downward/more uncertain after the final text.

Key mechanisms per SD Taxpayers:
- Application completeness deemed after 30 days
- 365 days EIR, 180 ND/MND, 90 exemption
- Narrowed alternatives: only one feasible alternative + no project
- 270-day judicial shot clock
- Standard of review: court may overturn only where agency ignored objective written standards in effect at application; substantial evidence deferential standard
- Severance remedy ("fix-it ticket")
- Bars late objections

That's an accurate summary of significant changes beyond timelines.

Now, my judgment. Let me think about this as a policy evaluation with expected consequences.

Arguments that this is net beneficial:
1. California's building cost/time problem is severe and well-documented (RAND: 2.5x Texas; Soltas & Gruber: permitting explains 1/3 of gap between home prices and construction costs in LA; permitting adds ~36% to construction cost). Reducing permitting friction has real, large economic benefits.
2. Nearly half of CEQA suits target taxpayer-funded public projects, so delays cost taxpayers directly.
3. Enforceable deadlines are a proven mechanism (federal FAST-41, state environmental leadership streamlining).
4. Substantive environmental laws remain (Clean Air/Water Acts, Coastal Act, ESA at federal level, state standards); agencies retain approval/denial authority; prevailing wage preserved for most categories.
5. The measure is optional for applicants.
6. Broad, diverse coalition; 26 newspaper endorsements; bipartisan (state GOP yes; some Dems like Buffy Wicks yes).

Arguments that this is net harmful:
1. 2. It cannot be fixed: 2/3 legislative vote and only "to further its purposes"; no sunset; frozen cross-references mean future environmental laws wouldn't apply to covered projects; plus a built-in continuous appropriation to defend it in court against the state's own elected officials.
3. Breadth: covers greenfield subdivisions, freeway expansions, logging, dams/irrigation, carbon capture, transmission, broadband/ancillary infrastructure (data centers disputed), warehouses as ancillary to housing? It reaches far beyond the housing problem the Legislature already addressed with AB 130/SB 131 (which is producing ~18k units in 15 months).
4. Equity/democracy: caps public comment at 45 days, excludes late comments from the judicial record, narrows tribes' consultation rights to federally recognized tribes (excluding most California tribes), weakens judicial remedies — reducing the main leverage EJ communities have.
5. Context: federal rollbacks under Trump (ESA habitat regs, NEPA) make state CEQA a more important backstop; locking it in weakened form now is risky.
6. Fiscal: LAO's final estimate says initial costs high tens of millions to >$100M annually; long-term effects uncertain and could be negative if harmful projects are approved.
7. Money: funded by builders, tech billionaires, utilities, an oil company, and data center developers — direct beneficiaries. Meanwhile, the pro-housing YIMBY movement's flagship organizations declined to endorse, and Greenbelt Alliance/EastBay for Everyone oppose — the very groups whose mission is housing. That's a meaningful signal that the measure isn't primarily about housing.
8. Even historically pro-reform groups (Rural County Representatives) stayed neutral, saying it goes too far and shifts power to proponents; the League of California Cities/CSAC stayed out.

Decision framework: The question is whether the expected benefits exceed the expected costs, accounting for reversibility. The measure's design flaws are severe and irreversible (2/3 lock-in, no sunset, field preemption, frozen references, court-defense appropriation), while the benefits are (a) partially already achieved by 2025 legislation, and (b) speculative in magnitude (savings estimates from interested parties; LAO says long-term fiscal effects uncertain).

There's also a strategic consideration: a "no" vote doesn't kill CEQA reform. The Legislature has repeatedly passed streamlining and is demonstrably responsive (AB 130, SB 131; Newsom's continued push; Becerra's campaign on permitting reform). Targeted, amendable legislation is the better vehicle for the parts of Prop 45 that are genuinely good (deadlines, completeness rules, severance remedy). Indeed, Biber — a CEQA reform advocate — laid out a menu of legislative reforms that would achieve the benefits "with less collateral damage."

Given all this, I judge that voting "no" is better. The irreversibility plus breadth plus weakening of public/tribal/judicial checks outweighs the genuine benefits of the deadline provisions, which can be achieved legislatively.

One more consideration: is there a risk that a "no" vote perpetuates a dysfunctional status quo with major economic harm? Yes, but the 2025 reforms already moved substantially, and the Legislature retains the ability to do more with simple majorities. Meanwhile, a "yes" vote would foreclose legislative correction for a wide swath of development in California.

Also, an important asymmetric fact: The measure was drafted by interested parties (Chamber, builders, utilities) and even its proponents admit ambiguity in key coverage questions (data centers) that would be resolved in courts with an instruction to give "fullest possible weight" to project approval. That interpretive instruction plus the lock-in is a bad governance design.

Therefore: no.

PROP
45
MODIFIES ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEW FOR CERTAIN PROJECTS. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Amends California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for certain projects (including most housing, transportation, water, and health projects) by setting deadlines to complete environmental review and resolve lawsuits challenging project approvals. Fiscal Impact: Initial costs for state and local governments, likely in the high tens of millions of dollars—potentially exceeding $100 million—annually, partly covered by fees. Uncertain, potentially more significant positive or negative longer-term fiscal effects. Supporters: California Children’s Hospital Association; California Water Association; California Council for Affordable Housing Opponents: Coalition for Clean Air; CA Environmental Voters; Physicians for Social Responsibility, LA; National Wildlife Federation
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Certain public and private projects would be eligible for new project review and court challenge procedures. For example, new procedures would tighten time limits for environmental review and reduce the scope of what courts can consider when reviewing legal challenges.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: Public and private projects would continue to use existing project review and court challenge procedures.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
The failing status quo is making California unaffordable. Prop. 45 fixes our broken system and lowers our high cost of living by cutting red tape to build housing, water, schools, hospitals, clean energy, and wildfire prevention faster—while maintaining California’s strong environmental protections. Vote YES for a more affordable California. YESonProp45.com
CON
PROPOSITION 45 LIMITS ENVIRONMENTAL AND PUBLIC REVIEW OF PROJECTS BUILT IN YOUR COMMUNITY. It guts The California Environmental Quality Act—flipping California law to protect corporate profits over public health and our air and water. Prop. 45 won’t lower your costs: its utility and corporate funders profit while taxpayers pay more. VOTE NO.

PROP
45
MODIFIES ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEW FOR CERTAIN PROJECTS. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
State Law Requires Government Agencies to Review the Environmental Impacts of Proposed Projects. State and local government agencies are responsible for reviewing and approving certain projects before they can be built. As part of this process, the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) requires an agency to consider how a project might negatively affect the environment before approving it. CEQA applies to many types of public and private projects, such as housing developments, school facilities, and highway expansions. Some exceptions apply. For example, state law exempts certain housing developments located near public transit from needing a CEQA review.
How the CEQA Process Works. The government agency first determines if CEQA applies to a project. If so, it then determines if the project could significantly affect the environment and if those impacts could be avoided or reduced with minor changes to the project. If making minor changes cannot avoid or reduce significant impacts, the agency must do a more detailed review called an environmental impact report (EIR). (The majority of projects do not require an EIR; however, EIRs are somewhat more common for large and complex projects.) The EIR analyzes possible environmental impacts the project could cause and considers alternatives that could reduce those impacts. After finishing the environmental review, the agency decides whether to approve the project. At certain times during this process, the government agency must seek and consider comments about the project’s environmental review from the public and other government agencies.
People Can Sue the Government Agency About Its CEQA Review. After a government agency has completed the CEQA review and decided whether to approve a project, people who think the agency did not follow the CEQA process correctly can sue the agency. For example, a project opponent might argue that the environmental analysis was inadequate. If the court finds that the agency did not follow CEQA correctly, it can stop the whole project and require the agency to fix the part of the process that was problematic.
Many Projects Also Need to Get Other Approvals. Besides CEQA review, many projects need approval or permits from other local and/or state government agencies before they can proceed. For example, a business that wants to build a health clinic might need the local government to change land use rules before it can proceed. It also may need state agencies to review and approve how the project might affect certain wildlife species and water quality.
PROPOSAL
Proposition 45 creates new procedures for reviewing certain types of projects that it defines as “essential.” Figure 1 lists the types of projects eligible for the new procedures. The proposition (1) tightens time limits for CEQA review, permits, and court challenges; (2) changes parts of the CEQA review process; and (3) changes the court’s review process for CEQA lawsuits. The proposition gives eligible project applicants the option of using the new procedures or existing procedures.
Tightens Time Limits for Review and Court Challenges of Eligible Projects. Proposition 45 creates more binding time limits for state and local governments to do both CEQA and permitting reviews. This includes time limits for determining if a project application is complete, finishing the EIR, and granting other types of approvals and permits. For example, Proposition 45 allows an applicant to request an agency hearing- and potentially file a lawsuit with the courts-if an agency does not meet the 365-business-day time limit for finishing the EIR. The proposition also creates a time limit for courts to resolve legal challenges.
Changes CEQA Review for Eligible Projects. For eligible projects, Proposition 45 makes several changes to the CEQA review process, including:
Application Process. Requires the government agency to specify all information that must be included in an application before it is submitted. (Current law allows agencies to repeatedly request additional information or project changes.)
How Environmental Impacts Are Assessed. Requires the agency to assess potential environmental impacts based on the laws and standards in place at the time the project application is submitted. (Current law lets the agency consider new information and revise its review standards when doing the EIR.)
Project Alternatives. Allows the applicant to develop only one project alternative for the agency to consider. (Current law requires the agency-not the applicant-to develop and consider multiple project alternatives that could reduce environmental impacts.)
Consultation With Native Tribes. Requires the agency and applicant to consult about the project only with California native tribes that have been formally recognized by the federal government. (Current law requires consultation with a wider range of tribes.)
Public Comment Periods. Limits how long the agency can accept comments from the public and other government agencies about the project. (Current law sets a minimum number of days-not a maximum-for public review.)
Changes How Courts Review Challenges to Eligible Projects. Proposition 45 makes several changes to the court’s review process when someone challenges a government agency’s approval of an eligible project. For example, it reduces the scope of what the court can consider in CEQA lawsuits. The proposition also prevents the court from stopping the whole project if it finds that the agency did not follow CEQA correctly. Instead, the court can only stop the part of the project where the environmental review did not comply with CEQA while the agency fixes the problem.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Initial Costs for State and Local Governments. During the first several years, Proposition 45 likely would increase costs for the state and local governments, including state courts. These costs likely would be in the high tens of millions of dollars annually, potentially exceeding $100 million annually . For example, state and local governments would have costs to develop new guidelines and standards for reviewing eligible projects’ environmental impacts, meet tighter time limits, and address court challenges. Fees paid by project applicants and people filing lawsuits would cover some of these costs. After this initial period, while some costs could continue, others likely would decline over time. For example, the changes to how courts can review CEQA lawsuits could mean fewer people will sue in the future, which could reduce costs for agencies and state courts in the long term.
In the Longer Term, Uncertain but Potentially More Significant Fiscal Effects. Proposition 45’s changes to project review and court challenge procedures for eligible projects could have various fiscal effects for state and local governments. The overall fiscal effect of these changes-positive or negative-is uncertain but could be more substantial than the near-term effects. For example, two effects that could have significant but uncertain impacts are:
More Projects and Faster Timing. To the degree that Proposition 45’s changes to project review and court challenge procedures lead to eligible public projects being constructed more quickly, state and local governments likely would have lower project costs. Additionally, if the proposition’s changes result in more projects being completed overall, it could lead to an increase in tax revenues, such as from property taxes.
Negative Environmental Impacts. To the degree that Proposition 45’s changes to project review and court challenge procedures lead to approval of projects with negative environmental impacts that would not have otherwise occurred, government agencies could face higher costs to respond to those impacts.

OFFICIAL TITLE AND SUMMARY
PREPARED BY THE ATTORNEY GENERAL
Amends California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for specified project categories (including most housing, transportation, water, health, wildfire mitigation, educational facility, internet access, and clean energy projects). For these types of projects, this measure:
Sets deadlines for public agencies to complete environmental review and take required actions.
Allows expedited review of environmental impacts, limiting public agencies’ current obligation to consider a range of feasible project alternatives to reduce environmental impacts.
Establishes deadlines for filing and resolving lawsuits challenging project approvals; limits evidence courts may consider and relief courts can order.
SUMMARY OF LEGISLATIVE ANALYST'S ESTIMATE OF NET STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT FISCAL IMPACT:
Initial costs for state and local governments, likely in the high tens of millions of dollars annually—potentially exceeding $100 million annually—to implement new project review and court challenge procedures for eligible projects. Fees paid by project applicants and people filing lawsuits would partly cover these costs.
In the longer term, uncertain, but potentially more significant positive or negative fiscal effects for state and local governments. The overall effect depends, in part, on how the new procedures change the number of eligible projects that get built and whether those projects have different environmental impacts.

California’s Prop 45 may be the biggest reform to CEQA in decades. Critics say it goes too far
By Kurtis Alexander (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/kurtis-alexander/) , Staff Writer Oct 2, 2026
The California Environmental Quality Act has long been blamed for stalling construction projects, but Proposition 45 seeks to change this.
Yalonda M. James/S.F. Chronicle
California has rolled back some of its notorious building regulations in recent years to battle long-standing problems of red tape and high costs.
Now, a measure on the November ballot is seeking to take the push for regulatory reform up a notch. Proposition 45, sponsored by the California Chamber of Commerce, would streamline the approval process for a wide range of development activities considered “essential,” from housing and highways to clean power projects and broadband internet. (Whether data centers are covered by the initiative remains a matter of legal debate.)

Critics of Proposition 45, which include many environmental groups, call the measure a giveaway for developers, utilities and corporations. They say it would weaken oversight and public input and go a step too far in the fight against bureaucracy.
At issue is the state’s bedrock land-use regulation, the California Environmental Quality Act, signed into law by Gov. Ronald Reagan in 1970. CEQA establishes a framework for protecting the environment by requiring state and local agencies to identify and limit the impacts of new development.
Proposition 45 would be perhaps the biggest reform to CEQA in its five-decade history.
The law has long helped stave off problems for communities, wild spaces and ecosystems and, as such, has been praised for enhancing California’s natural landscapes and quality of life. But CEQA is also blamed for obstructing needed work, and critics have no shortage of examples of when the regulation has brought seemingly endless delays and frivolous lawsuits.

“It’s egregious to suggest we need housing proposals to go on for 10 years and we need a decade of public comments,” said Jason Elliott, a longtime policy guru and onetime adviser to Gov. Gavin Newsom. Elliott helped write Proposition 45.
Over the years, state lawmakers have pushed through many changes to try to improve CEQA, including last year’s high-profile legislation urged by the governor that resulted in regulatory exemptions for urban infill housing projects, to help move them along. Other amendments to the law have been mostly smaller statutory fixes or carve-outs for specific developments.
Across 41 pages, Proposition 45 — officially titled “Modifies Environmental Review for Certain Projects” by the attorney general — lays out several modifications to the law that would make applying for new development easier, establish binding deadlines for consideration of proposed projects and narrow the ability of the courts to weigh in on the process.
For example, developers wouldn’t have to propose and analyze multiple alternatives to their project, like they do now, just one. Also, public agencies would have a deadline of 365 days to complete project reviews, known as environmental impact reports, under the threat of a public hearing or legal action.
Elliott and other supporters say the measure wouldn’t lower regulatory standards, just speed things up and keep costs down.

They also note that projects eligible for streamlining would be limited, though several categories of development would qualify: housing, water infrastructure, clean energy, health services, wildfire prevention, broadband internet, education facilities and transportation.
Opponents of the proposition say so many changes for so many projects is an invitation for sprawl and polluting development. They worry that fast-tracking the approval process would inevitably lead to less comprehensive reviews and public comment, resulting in projects that yield toxic emissions, increase wildfire risk and squeeze energy and water supplies.
They argue now is an especially bad time to roll back oversight, given the federal government’s sweeping deregulatory agenda under President Donald Trump.
“I remain very concerned that we are not adequately protecting the environment because there’s so much backsliding happening (not only) when it comes to fighting climate change, but also in our land-use decisions and policies,” said Democratic state Sen. Catherine Blakespear, who represents parts of San Diego and Orange counties and chairs the Senate Environmental Quality Committee.
Blakespear has come out against Proposition 45, as has the state Democratic Party, though polling by the Public Policy Institute of California shows that Democratic voters are split on the measure. The Republican Party has endorsed it.

The PPIC poll, conducted last month, also shows the proposition in a close race among all voters. The yes vote held a slight advantage.
While reforming CEQA has been popular, even among some critics of the proposition, the opposition maintains that changes should be done surgically by lawmakers, not with an expansive policy at the ballot box.
“The Legislature has proven over the past decade that they are more than willing to tackle CEQA abuse,” said Jordan Grimes, legislative director at the nonprofit Greenbelt Alliance.
The pro-housing group California YIMBY (Yes In My Back Yard) has taken a neutral position on Proposition 45, saying the scope of the measure, and its ramifications, go well beyond building new homes.
The proposition, Grimes and others say, is so broad that it could allow data centers to be fast-tracked, qualifying as an eligible broadband internet facility under terms of the measure. The architects of the proposition claim otherwise, saying the controversial enterprises are excluded. The backers accuse the opposition of trying to tie data centers to the measure for political purposes.

Specifically listed as ineligible for faster review are the contentious water tunnel proposal in the Sacramento-San Joaquin River Delta and California’s high-speed rail project.
Supporters of the initiative have raised about twice as much money as the opposition, state records show. The campaign’s funding has come largely from business, construction and housing interests. The biggest financial backer is Building a Better California, a campaign committee founded by tech leaders that’s also helping finance opposition to California’s proposed billionaire tax.
The opposition is getting much of its money from environmental groups and unions, according to state records. Philanthropist and investor Wendy Schmidt, who is married to former Google CEO Eric Schmidt, has also given significantly. (Her husband has given to the Building a Better California committee.).
Alex Jackson, executive director of the trade association American Clean Power — California, which supports Proposition 45, argues that a yes vote is the right environmental choice because the measure is key to the state’s fight against climate change.
“To meet the climate challenge, we need to build clean energy infrastructure at pace and scale,” he said. “This (measure) will meaningfully streamline the projects that the state is counting on.”

Powerful Interests Aim to Weaken California’s Landmark Environmental Law
Utilities, developers and technology companies have spent tens of millions to pass Prop 45, which fast-tracks “essential” projects by limiting public and environmental review.
By Liza Gross (https://insideclimatenews.org/profile/liza-gross/)

Political action committees funded by technology companies, the state’s major utilities and other corporate interests have spent several million dollars more to pass a ballot measure that would greenlight major development projects with minimal environmental or public review than public interest and labor groups have spent opposing it.
Developers and other corporate interests aim to streamline the California Environmental Quality Act, or CEQA (https://www.califaep.org/docs/CEQA_Handbook_2023_final.pdf), which requires public agencies to identify, disclose and mitigate a development project’s negative impacts on a wide range of environmental resources, including wildlife, air and water quality and tribal cultural resources.
Proposition 45 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop45-text-proposed-laws.pdf) shifts who determines the scope of environmental review from public agencies and communities to project developers by rewriting the state’s foundational environmental law to fast-track major projects.
Supporters of Prop 45, sponsored by the California Chamber of Commerce, have spent at least $36 million to pass the measure, the most recent state records show. Opponents, led by a coalition of more than 550 labor, health and environmental organizations, have spent about $30 million to defeat what they say will give polluters a free pass.

“Prop 45 will modernize the approval process for essential projects by establishing clear, enforceable timelines for agency decisions and court challenges,” the chamber said in promotional materials, “while keeping environmental protections intact and preserving worker protections, tribal protections and local control.”
Critics say Prop 45 will gut the state’s primary vehicle for allowing people to learn about plans for polluting developments in their neighborhoods and propose alternatives.
“It undermines basically every stage of that process,” said Woody Little, the spokesperson for No on Prop 45.
Little and his allies say the 41-page ballot measure (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0023A1%20%28%26quot%3BEssential%20Projects%26quot%3B%29.pdf) was written by corporations who have paid to get their special interests on the ballot to create loopholes that favor polluting industries like recently regulated (https://www.gov.ca.gov/2026/09/21/governor-newsom-signs-most-comprehensive-data-center-laws-in-the-nation-providing-communities-more-control-on-water-electricity-and-land-use/) data centers while limiting the input of communities and local tribes.
Critics of CEQA, signed in 1970 by then-Gov. Ronald Reagan, blame the law for hobbling home construction and driving housing and cost of living increases in California, which are among the highest in the nation.
Prop 45 will lower housing and utility costs by reducing “endless” bureaucratic delays and protect taxpayers by reducing waste and cost overruns, Yes on Prop 45 materials argue.
Yet there is no requirement in the measure to reduce housing costs or utility bills. And the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=45&year=2026) estimates that Prop 45 could leave state and local governments paying $100 million or more a year, partly to cover fast-tracked projects’ environmental impacts.
“The housing issue is a smokescreen for all these other polluting projects,” said Little.
California passed laws last year that significantly streamlined CEQA by exempting (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260AB130) urban and mixed-use housing construction from its provisions as well as certain infrastructure (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB131) and clean energy (https://www.energy.ca.gov/programs-and-topics/topics/power-plants/opt-certification-program) projects.
“ I would hope that 100 percent of Californians would see this radical reshaping of California’s environmental law for the dangerous thing that it is. A wolf in sheep’s clothing.”
— Woody Little, No on Prop 45
None of the grassroots groups that promote “yes in my backyard,” or YIMBY (https://yimbyaction.org/), policies to build more housing and public transit in urban and suburban areas support Prop 45, Little said. Most are neutral, he said, while others oppose it.
Expanding housing beyond already developed areas means building new freeways, water connections and other expensive infrastructure that taxpayers ultimately pay for, Little said. And these projects often encroach on the wildland-urban interface, raising wildfire risk just as climate change is making fires more destructive.
At a time when California is already seeing the catastrophic costs of climate-fueled fires, Little said, the state should be requiring more environmental review around developments to assess and mitigate risk, not less.
What’s “Essential”?
Prop 45 covers nine types of “essential” projects, among them housing, water systems, clean energy (including carbon capture and storage), transportation, wildfire risk reduction and broadband internet access. All related and “ancillary” infrastructure is also covered.
Whether “ancillary” includes data centers, which typically require broadband infrastructure (https://tiaonline.org/how-broadband-workforce-development-and-standards-drive-data-center-growth/), has been a major point of contention.
Prop 45’s proponents have insisted the measure does not cover data centers, but legal experts disagree, pointing to $2 million in donations from just three data center builders and language buried in the measure’s 41 pages. Eligible projects include “broadband internet access projects,” defined as “mass-market retail service … that provides the capability to transmit data to, and receive data from, all or substantially all Internet endpoints,” a recent analysis (https://www.dailyjournal.com/articles/394431-prop-45-will-speed-data-center-construction) found.
